Derived Associative Algebras and Cyclic Cohomology of Q-manifolds

Andrew James Bruce   Address: Independent Researcher, Cardiff, United Kingdom Email address: andrewjamesbruce@googlemail.com
Date: September 4, 2026
Abstract.

Loday’s derived product is revisited in the setting of Q-manifolds, i.e., supermanifolds equipped with an odd vector field that ‘squares to zero’. We interpret the Grassmann odd product as a standard product upon shifting the grading, which implies the existence of a derived (noncommutative) associative ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-graded algebra associated with any Q-manifold. We apply Connes’ cyclic cohomology to the derived associative algebra, giving a new cohomology on Q-manifolds distinct from the standard cohomology: we refer to this as the derived cyclic cohomology of a Q-manifold. The derived cyclic cocycles are interpreted as classically BRST-invariant functionals within the BV–BFV–BRST formalism or generalised Ruelle–Sullivan currents when applied to regular foliations via their foliation Lie algebroids.
Keywords: Q-manifolds; Derived Associative Algebras; Derived Cyclic Cohomology; BV–BRST Mechanics

1. Introduction and Background

1.1. Introduction

Q-manifolds, that is, supermanifolds equipped with an integrable odd vector field, are found in many areas of mathematical physics and differential geometry. Specifically, Q-manifolds arise in the theory of Lie algebroids, Poisson geometry, Courant algebroids, L∞L_{\infty}-algebroids, and related settings. Even the de Rham complex and Cartan calculus have a very natural formulation in terms of a Q-manifold. From the perspective of this paper, Q-manifolds (or their infinite-dimensional generalisations) appear in physics via the BV--BFV--BRST11 1 Batalin–Vilkovisky, Batalin–Fradkin–Vilkovisky, and Becchi–Rouet–Stora–Tyutin. formalism, see [1, 38]. The philosophy we adopt is that Q-manifolds provide a simplified environment to uncover mathematical aspects of the BV–BRST formalism in field theory. More correctly, we view Q-manifolds through the lens of BRST gauge mechanics by interpreting the homological vector field as the BRST differential; see [18], for example. By restricting attention to finite-dimensional supermanifolds, we avoid the technical issues with field theory.

It must be stressed that BRST symmetry, and thus BRST-cohomology, is vital in the consistent quantisation of gauge theories, general relativity (as an effective theory), and string theory. In particular, local BRST-cohomology and the descent equations are the foundation of the modern understanding of anomalies; see Bertlmann [2] for a review. Q-manifolds are vital in the AKSZ construction of sigma models, see [1]; and so fundamental in Kontsevich’s work on deformation quantisation of Poisson manifolds, see [24]. We also remark that Q-manifolds provide concrete, finite-dimensional (local) models for derived manifolds within derived differential geometry, see [8]. In short, Q-manifolds are ubiquitous across geometric approaches to physics and modern differential geometry.

In this paper, we revisit Loday’s derived product/multiplication on a differential graded algebra in the geometric setting of Q-manifolds. Loday’s motivation (see [28]) was the construction of associative dialgebras in order to build Leibniz–Loday algebras, i.e., ‘non-skew-symmetric Lie algebras’. The core idea of this paper is to take the construction of a derived multiplication as a stand-alone notion. The subtlety is that any such derived product f⋆g=±Q⁡(f)​gf\star g=\pm Q(f)g, where QQ is a differential (homological vector field), carries non-zero Grassmann parity. In short, we have an associative odd multiplication. That is, the Grassmann parity of the product of two functions is the sum of Grassmann parities of the functions, plus one. Another immediate complication is that the lack of a unit element for the derived product.

Odd multiplication is already an exotic notion and seems discordant with standard graded algebra. We will show that this can be largely remedied by employing a shifted grading which renders the derived product a standard ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded associative algebra. We stress that this shifted grading is formal in the sense that it is just a relabelling of even and odd functions. We are not constructing a new supermanifold using this shift; we have a bookkeeping device to track the sign factors consistently. Thus, by employing a shifted grading, the global functions on a Q-manifold come equipped with a derived associative algebra, which is a standard associative superalgebra with respect to the shifted grading. We further stress that the derived associative algebra associated with a Q-manifold is not (super)commutative. Thus, the core ethos of this work is the following:

What happens if we treat the derived product on a Q-manifold with the machinery of noncommutative geometry22 2 See, for example [11, 17, 34, 35] for introductions to noncommutative geometry.?

We remark that odd forms of multiplication can be found in the setting of Stasheff’s A∞A_{\infty}-algebras (strongly homotopy associative algebras) via suspension/shift. That is, the even binary operation m2:A⊗A→Am_{2}:A\otimes A\rightarrow A can be shifted to an odd binary operation b2:A⁡[1]⊗A⁡[1]→A⁡[1]b_{2}:A[1]\otimes A[1]\rightarrow A[1]. This may be understood in terms of the operadic suspension, i.e., the operad whose operations have been shifted in homological degree and the appropriate sign factors inserted. For an introduction to A∞A_{\infty}-algebras, the reader may consult Keller [22]. The bar-cobar construction linking dg-algebras and dg-coalgebras similarly requires a suspension/shift. For an introduction to the bar-cobar construction, the reader may consult [29, Chapter 2].

We apply Connes’ (topological) cyclic cohomology, suitably ‘superised’ following Kastler [20], to the derived associative algebra associated with any Q-manifold. In doing so, we obtain a cohomology theory quite independent of the standard cohomology of a Q-manifold: this cohomology theory we refer to as the derived cyclic cohomology of a Q-manifold. While the calculation of cyclic cohomology groups for general noncommutative algebras is notoriously difficult, we present some simple examples of derived cyclic zeroth-cohomology groups. The zeroth cohomology is interpreted within the finite-dimensional BV–BRST formalism as equivalence classes of classically BRST-invariant functionals τ:C∞​(M)→ℝ\tau:C^{\infty}(M)\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}. Mathematically, these functionals are Q-invariant in the sense that τ∘Q=0\tau\circ Q=0. Similarly, the higher cohomology groups are interpreted as equivalence classes of BRST-invariant derived cyclic multi-functionals. We apply this machinery to regular foliations via their foliation Lie algebroid and show that the derived cyclic 00-cocycles include Ruelle–Sullivan currents (see [37]). Moreover, we construct derived cyclic nn-cocycles associated with a regular foliation.

We emphasise that the descriptor ‘derived’ used throughout this work indicates derived in the sense of Loday, i.e., the structures are built from a standard one and a differential. It should not be confused with the related notion found within the complementary framework of derived algebraic geometry (see [14] for an introduction).

Organisation: We continue this introductory section with Subsection 1.2 in which the fundamental aspects of the theory of Q-manifolds are recalled. In Section 2 we define the derived product and explore its properties. In Section 3 we move on to the derived cyclic cohomology. We end with some concluding remarks and open questions in Section 4.

1.2. Recollection of Q-manifolds

We will assume that the reader has a grasp of the basic theory of supermanifolds. A supermanifold M:=(|M|,𝒪M)M:=(|M|,\>\mathcal{O}_{M}) of dimension n|mn|m, we understand to be a supermanifold as defined by Berezin & Leites [3, 27]. That is, a supermanifold is a locally superringed space that is locally isomorphic to ℝn|m:=(ℝn,Cℝn∞(−)⊗Λ(¸1,⋯¸m))\mathbb{R}^{n|m}:=\big({\mathbb{R}}^{n},C^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}(-)\otimes\Lambda(\mathchar 28952\relax^{1},\cdots\mathchar 28952\relax^{m})\big). Here, Cℝn∞​(−)C^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}(-) is the sheaf of smooth real functions on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and Λ(¸1,⋯¸m)\Lambda(\mathchar 28952\relax^{1},\cdots\mathchar 28952\relax^{m}) is the Grassmann algebra (over ℝ{\mathbb{R}}) with mm generators. The underlying topological space |M||M| is, in fact, a smooth manifold. This manifold we refer to as the reduced manifold. Morphisms of supermanifolds are morphisms as superringed spaces. That is, a morphism φ:M→N\varphi:M\rightarrow N consists of a pair φ=(|φ|,φ∗)\varphi=(|\varphi|,\varphi^{*}), where |φ|:|M|→|N||\varphi|:|M|\rightarrow|N| is a continuous map (in fact, smooth) and φ∗\varphi^{*} is a family of superring homomorphisms φ|V|∗:𝒪N​(|V|)→𝒪M​(|φ|−1​(|V|))\varphi^{*}_{|V|}:\mathcal{O}_{N}(|V|)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{M}\big(|\varphi|^{-1}(|V|)\big), for every open |V|⊂|N||V|\subset|N|, that respect the restriction maps. The category of supermanifolds we denote as SMan. We will set C∞​(M):=𝒪M​(|M|)C^{\infty}(M):=\mathcal{O}_{M}(|M|). An important and useful result is that

𝖧𝗈𝗆SMan​(M1,M2)≅𝖧𝗈𝗆SAlg​(C∞​(M2),C∞​(M1)).{Hom}_{\textnormal{{SMan}}}(M_{1},M_{2})\cong{Hom}_{\textnormal{{SAlg}}}\big(C^{\infty}(M_{2}),C^{\infty}(M_{1})\big)\,.

where SAlg is the category of unital, supercommutative, associative algebras. This allows one to understand morphisms of supermanifolds in terms of homomorphisms between the algebras of global sections. Via minor abuse of notation, we set φ∗:C∞​(M2)→C∞​(M1)\varphi^{*}:C^{\infty}(M_{2})\rightarrow C^{\infty}(M_{1}) for the algebra homomorphism associated with a supermanifold homomorphism. For an introduction to supermanifolds, the reader may consult Carmeli et al. [9].

A Q-manifold, following Schwarz [38] circa late 1992, is a supermanifold equipped with an odd vector field Q∈𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(M)Q\in{Vect}(M) that satisfies the integrability condition [Q,Q]=0[Q,Q]=0. Such vector fields are referred to as homological vector fields as (C∞​(M),Q)(C^{\infty}(M),Q) is a differential algebra. We remark that non-trivial homological vector fields only exist on supermanifolds with non-zero odd dimension, i.e., that cannot exist on pure even manifolds. It should be noted that the notion of a homological vector field on a supermanifold goes back to at least 1980 and is attributed to Shander [39]. We also highlight the foundational contribution of Vaintrob [43]. Note that the action of QQ extends from C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M) to the tensor algebra via the Lie derivative ℒQ\mathcal{L}_{Q}.

Morphisms of Q-manifolds, which we refer to as Q-morphisms, are morphisms of supermanifolds φ:M1→M2\varphi:M_{1}\rightarrow M_{2}, such that

Q1∘φ∗−φ∗∘Q2=0.Q_{1}\circ\varphi^{*}-\varphi^{*}\circ Q_{2}=0\,.

We say that Q1Q_{1} and Q2Q_{2} are φ\varphi-related. In this way we obtain the category of Q-manifolds, which we will denote as QMan. Isomorphisms in the category of Q-manifolds are obviously defined, and we refer to them as Q-diffeomorphisms.

Example 1.1.

Any supermanifold or manifold may be equipped with the zero homological vector field. We will refer to such Q-manifolds as trivial Q-manifolds.

Example 1.2.

Let NN be a pure even manifold; then we can identify (generally inhomogeneous) differential forms as functions on the odd tangent bundle Π​𝖳​N\Pi{{T}}N. That is, we have the natural isomorphism Ω∙​(N)≅C∞​(Π​𝖳​N)\Omega^{\bullet}(N)\cong C^{\infty}(\Pi{{T}}N). The de Rham differential is identified with a homological vector field and so (Π​𝖳​N,d)(\Pi{{T}}N,\textnormal{d}) is a Q-manifold.

Example 1.3.

By replacing the tangent bundle with a Lie algebroid (A,[−,−],ρ)(A,[-,-],\rho), we obtain the Q-manifold (Π​A,dA)(\Pi A,\textnormal{d}_{A}), where dA\textnormal{d}_{A} is the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential of the Lie algebroid. See Vaintrob [44] for details.

Example 1.4.

Let (N,P)(N,P) be a Poisson manifold. We can interpret the Poisson bivector as a function on the odd cotangent bundle Π​𝖳∗​N\Pi{{T}}^{*}N, and the Schouten–Nijenhuis bracket is identified with the canonical odd Poisson bracket. The Poisson condition [[P,P]]SN=0[\hskip-1.5pt[P,P]\hskip-1.5pt]_{\textrm{SN}}=0, implies that δ:=[[P,−]]SN\delta:=[\hskip-1.5pt[P,-]\hskip-1.5pt]_{\textrm{SN}} is a homological vector field. The homological vector field δ\delta is identified with the Lichnerowicz differential. For an introduction to Poisson geometry, the reader may consult [12].

We remark that the category QMan is a Cartesian monoidal category (see Mac Lane [33, Section VII]). If (M1,Q1)(M_{1},Q_{1}) and (M2,Q2)(M_{2},Q_{2}) are Q-manifolds then (M:=M1×M2,Q:=Q1+Q2)(M:=M_{1}\times M_{2},Q:=Q_{1}+Q_{2}) is again a Q-manifold, and the monoidal unit is (ℝ0|0,𝟎)({\mathbb{R}}^{0|0},\mathbf{0}).

A homological vector field on a supermanifold we can interpret as a smooth action of the additive supergroup ℝ0|1{\mathbb{R}}^{0|1}, which we equip with the odd coordinate θ\theta. The action 𝖺:ℝ0|1×M→M\mathsf{a}:{\mathbb{R}}^{0|1}\times M\rightarrow M corresponds to the algebra map 𝖺∗:C∞​(M)→Λ⁡(θ)⊗C∞​(M)\mathsf{a}^{*}:C^{\infty}(M)\rightarrow\Lambda(\theta)\otimes C^{\infty}(M), which we write as

(1.1) 𝖺∗​f:=f+θ​Q​(f),\mathsf{a}^{*}f:=f+\theta\,Q(f)\,,

for any f∈C∞​(M)f\in C^{\infty}(M). One can check that the group actions axioms hold provided Q2=0Q^{2}=0. We then interpret this action as the “odd flow” generated by QQ. In more physical language, we think of BRST transformations, and θ\theta plays the role of an “odd gauge parameter”. For details of Lie supergroups and actions, see Carmeli et al. [9, Chapter 7 and Chapter 8]

The set of Q-closed functions (Q-cocycles) we denote by 𝒵⁡(M,Q):=ker⁡(Q)\mathcal{Z}(M,Q):=\ker(Q), and the set of Q-exact functions (Q-boundaries) as ℬ​(M,Q):=Im​(Q)\mathcal{B}(M,Q):=\textrm{Im}(Q). The standard cohomology33 3 In the BRST formalism, the standard cohomology is identified (modulo ghost number) as the BRST-cohomology. of (M,Q)(M,Q) is defined as Hstd∙​(M,Q):=𝒵⁡(M,Q)/ℬ⁡(M,Q)H^{\bullet}_{\textnormal{std}}(M,Q):=\mathcal{Z}(M,Q)/\mathcal{B}(M,Q). Note that we have a two-term complex labelled by the Grassmann parity. For more information about the standard cohomology and characteristic classes, the reader may consult Lyakhovich et al. [31]. For an overview of homological algebra, the reader may consult Weibel [47].

Example 1.5.

Let NN be a pure even manifold; then the standard cohomology of (Π​𝖳​N,d)(\Pi{{T}}N,\textnormal{d}) is identified with the (ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded) de Rham cohomology of NN.

In practice, the structure sheaf of a Q-manifold is often ℤ2×ℕ{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}\times\mathbb{N} or ℤ2×ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}\times{\mathbb{Z}} graded; the additional grading, which we refer to as weight44 4 More generally, the structure sheaf is ℤ2×ℕn{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}\times\mathbb{N}^{n} or ℤ2×ℤn{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}\times{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} graded and we have a multi-weight. For example, in the BV–BRST formalism there are ghost and antifield numbers, etc. to contend with.. The homological vector field is usually of weight +1+1. In this paper, weight will play no explicit role. Thus, we will suppress the weight and work with the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-grading only, which, in general, is independent of the weight. For example, within the BRST formalism applied to gauge mechanics, the weight may be identified with ghost number.

We will drop explicit reference to super, and understand all objects to be ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded. For example, by associative algebra we will mean associative superalgebra, and by Lie algebra we will mean Lie superalgebra, etc.

We will, as common in supergeometry, use ℝn|m{\mathbb{R}}^{n|m} to denote the supermanifold (ℝn,Cℝn∞(−)⊗Λ(¸1,⋯¸m)))\big({\mathbb{R}}^{n},C^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}(-)\otimes\Lambda(\mathchar 28952\relax^{1},\cdots\mathchar 28952\relax^{m})\big)) as well as the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded vector space ℝn⊕ℝm{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\oplus{\mathbb{R}}^{m}. The context should make the meaning clear.

2. The Derived Algebra of a Q-manifold

2.1. The Derived Associative Algebra

Following Loday [28] (also see Uchino [42] for higher versions, and Bruce [5, Section 6] for earlier work on the derived product on a Q-manifold), we make the following definition, taking into account the Grassmann parity of functions on a Q-manifold.

Definition 2.1.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold. Then the derived product/multiplication is the ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-bilinear map

⋆:C∞​(M)×C∞​(M)⟶C∞​(M),\star:C^{\infty}(M)\times C^{\infty}(M)\longrightarrow C^{\infty}(M)\,,

defined as f⋆g:=(−1)f~​Q​(f)​gf\star g:=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q(f)\,g, for all f,g∈C∞​(M)f,g\in C^{\infty}(M).

Derived products should be viewed as the associative cousin of derived brackets; see Kosmann-Schwarzbach [25] and references therein. For example, it is well known that on any Q-manifold [X,Y]Q:=(−1)X~​[[Q,X],Y][X,Y]_{Q}:=(-1)^{\widetilde{X}}\,[[Q,X],Y] defines an odd Loday–Leibniz bracket on 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(M){Vect}(M).

Proposition 2.1.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold; the derived multiplication (see Definition 2.1) is

  1. i)

    Grassmann odd, i.e., f⋆g~=f~+g~+1\widetilde{f\star g}=\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{g}+1; and

  2. ii)

    Associative, i.e., (f⋆g)⋆h=f⋆(g⋆h)(f\star g)\star h=f\star(g\star h).

Proof.

  1. i)

    This is clear as Q~=1\widetilde{Q}=1.

  2. ii)

    This requires a short calculation.

    (f⋆g)⋆h=(−1)f~+f~+1+g~​Q​(Q⁡(f)​g)​h=(−1)f~+g~​Q​(f)​Q​(g)​h=f⋆(g⋆h),(f\star g)\star h=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{f}+1+\widetilde{g}}\,Q\big(Q(f)g\big)h=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{g}}\,Q(f)Q(g)h=f\star(g\star h)\,,

    with f,g,h∈C∞​(M)f,g,h\in C^{\infty}(M). Note we have used Q2=0Q^{2}=0.

∎

We will refer to (C∞​(M),+,⋆)(C^{\infty}(M),+,\star) as the derived associative algebra of (M,Q)(M,Q), noting that under the shifted grading f¯:=f~+1\overline{f}:=\widetilde{f}+1 we have a standard ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded associative algebra. In particular, f⋆g~=f~+g~+1\widetilde{f\star g}=\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{g}+1, which implies

(2.1) f⋆g¯=f¯+1+g¯+1=f¯+g¯.\overline{f\star g}=\overline{f}+1+\overline{g}+1=\overline{f}+\overline{g}\,.

That is, with respect to the shifted grading, the derived product is even. For brevity, we will on occasion write (C∞​(M),⋆)(C^{\infty}(M),\star) or (C∞(M),⋆Q)(C^{\infty}(M),\star_{Q}) for the derived associative algebra.

Recall that C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M) with its usual product is a nuclear Frećhet algebra (see Carmeli et al. [9, Chapter 4.5] for details). Specifically, the usual product is jointly continuous. As QQ is a derivation of sections of the structure sheaf, the map f↦Q⁡(f)f\mapsto Q(f) is continuous with respect to the standard Frećhet topology on C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M). Thus, the derived product f⋆g=±Q⁡(f)​gf\star g=\pm\,Q(f)\,g is jointly continuous, and so the derived associative algebra is a nuclear Frećhet algebra. For details of functional analysis, we defer to Trèves [41].

In light of Loday’s dialgebras, we may consider another derived associative product given by f⋆′g:=f​Q​(g)f\star^{\prime}g:=f\,Q(g). However, as the underlying algebra is supercommutative, a quick calculation shows that f⋆′g=−(−1)f¯​g¯g⋆ff\star^{\prime}g=-(-1)^{\bar{f}\,\bar{g}}\,g\star f. Thus, these two derived associative algebras are (shifted) anti-opposite algebras.

We are not employing the parity reversion functor and considering Π​C∞​(M)\Pi C^{\infty}(M) (as the underlying vector space). One may use the parity reversion functor to exchange even and odd forms of associative multiplication. However, attempting to do so here would destroy the geometric nature of the constructions, i.e., the algebraic structure is not guaranteed to be the algebra of functions on a supermanifold. Rather, we are shifting the labelling of the grading to allow direct application of standard ideas from ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded algebra. It is important to note that the derived associative algebra is not (shifted or otherwise) graded commutative. The noncommutativity is clear due to the ‘lopsided’ definition of the derived product.

Example 2.1.

Let MM be a (super)manifold considered as a trivial Q-manifold, i.e., the homological vector field is the zero vector field. In this case, the shifted product defines a zero or null associative algebra. That is, f⋆g=0f\star g=0 for all functions f,g∈C∞​(M)f,g\in C^{\infty}(M).

Example 2.2.

A finite-dimensional version of the classical BV formalism is modelled by higher Poisson structures (see [45]). A higher Poisson manifold is a supermanifold MM equipped with an even multivector field 𝒫∈C∞​(Π​𝖳∗​M)\mathcal{P}\in C^{\infty}(\Pi{{T}}^{*}M) such that [[𝒫,𝒫]]=0[\hskip-1.5pt[\mathcal{P},\mathcal{P}]\hskip-1.5pt]=0, where [[−,−]][\hskip-1.5pt[-,-]\hskip-1.5pt] is the canonical odd Poisson bracket on Π​𝖳∗​M\Pi{{T}}^{*}M: in the classical setting the odd Poisson bracket is identified with the Schouten–Nijenhuis bracket. The higher Poisson structure 𝒫\mathcal{P} is interpreted as a ‘classical extended action ’; the odd symplectic self-commuting condition is interpreted as the ‘classical master equation’, and the bracket itself is interpreted as the antibracket. The derived product is given by 𝒳⋆𝒴=(−1)𝒳~​[[𝒫,𝒳]]​𝒴\mathcal{X}\star\mathcal{Y}=(-1)^{\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}}\,[\hskip-1.5pt[\mathcal{P},\mathcal{X}]\hskip-1.5pt]\,\mathcal{Y}, for all 𝒳,𝒴∈C∞​(Π​𝖳∗​M)\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}\in C^{\infty}(\Pi{{T}}^{*}M).

Example 2.3.

Let NN be a smooth manifold; then differential forms on NN are understood as functions on M:=Π​𝖳​NM:=\Pi{{T}}N and the de Rham differential is understood as a homological vector field. Thus, Ω∙​(N)≅C∞​(Π​𝖳​N)\Omega^{\bullet}(N)\cong C^{\infty}(\Pi{{T}}N). The shifted product is

α⋆β=(−1)α~​d​α∧β.\alpha\star\beta=(-1)^{\widetilde{\alpha}}\,\textnormal{d}\alpha\wedge\beta\,.

Suppose α\alpha is a nowhere vanishing one-form. Then via the Frobenius Theorem, we note that if

α⋆α=−d​α∧α=0,\alpha\star\alpha=-\textnormal{d}\alpha\wedge\alpha=0\,,

then ker⁡(α)\ker(\alpha) defines a completely integrable distribution. Generalising this, suppose we have r<dimNr<\dim N (point-wise) linearly independent one-forms {α1,α2,⋯,αr}\{\alpha^{1},\alpha^{2},\cdots,\alpha^{r}\}. Let us define Ω:=α1∧α2∧⋯∧αr\Omega:=\alpha^{1}\wedge\alpha^{2}\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha^{r}. The Frobenius Theorem can then be stated as

αi⋆Ω=0,\alpha^{i}\star\Omega=0\,,

with 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r.

Example 2.4.

In the theory of (finite-dimensional) gauge systems, the BRST differential is recognised as a homological vector field on the supermanifold of configurations, ghosts and antifields, etc. A little more carefully, we have a triple (M,{−,−}ϵ,𝒬ϵ+1)\big(M,\{-,-\}_{\epsilon},\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1}\big) where the Poisson bracket is of Grassmann parity ϵ∈ℤ2\epsilon\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}, and the homological potential 𝒬ϵ+1∈C∞​(M)\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1}\in C^{\infty}(M) is of Grassmann parity ϵ+1\epsilon+1. The BRST differential is defined as Q={𝒬ϵ+1,−}ϵQ=\{\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1},-\}_{\epsilon}, which requires the classical master equation {𝒬ϵ+1,𝒬ϵ+1}ϵ=0\{\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1},\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1}\}_{\epsilon}=0 to hold. For details, the reader may consult [18] and/or [30]. The derived product is thus

f⋆g=(−1)f~​{𝒬ϵ+1,f}​g=(−1)ϵ+1​Xf​(𝒬ϵ+1)​g,f\star g=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,\{\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1},f\}\,g=(-1)^{\epsilon+1}\,X_{f}(\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1})\,g\,,

where we define the Hamiltonian vector field Xf:={f,−}ϵX_{f}:=\{f,-\}_{\epsilon}. We remark that if ff and 𝒬ϵ+1\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1} are in involution, then f⋆g=0f\star g=0.

Proposition 2.2.

Let (M1,Q1)(M_{1},Q_{1}) and (M2,Q2)(M_{2},Q_{2}) be Q-manifolds and φ:M1→M2\varphi:M_{1}\rightarrow M_{2} be a morphism of Q-manifolds. Then φ∗:C∞​(M2)→C∞​(M1)\varphi^{*}:C^{\infty}(M_{2})\rightarrow C^{\infty}(M_{1}) is a derived associative algebra homomorphism.

Proof.

Linearity is automatic by the definition of the pullback. We only need to check the behaviour of the pullback on the derived product of two functions.

φ∗​(f⋆2g)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(f\star_{2}g) =φ∗​((−1)f~​Q2​(f)​g)=(−1)f~​φ∗​(Q2​(f))​φ∗​g\displaystyle=\varphi^{*}\big((-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q_{2}(f)g\big)=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,\varphi^{*}\big(Q_{2}(f)\big)\varphi^{*}g
=(−1)f~​Q1​(φ∗​f)​φ∗​g=φ∗​f⋆1φ∗​g,\displaystyle=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q_{1}(\varphi^{*}f)\varphi^{*}g=\varphi^{*}f\star_{1}\varphi^{*}g\,,

where we have used Q1∘φ∗=φ∗∘Q2Q_{1}\circ\varphi^{*}=\varphi^{*}\circ Q_{2}. ∎

Proposition 2.2 tells us that we have a functor 𝒪der:QManop→NUSAlg\mathcal{O}_{\textrm{der}}:\textnormal{{QMan}}^{\textrm{op}}\rightarrow\textnormal{{NUSAlg}} (non-unital associative superalgebras) via the construction of the derived associative algebra.

Example 2.5.

A morphism of gauge systems (see Example 2.4) (M,{−,−}ϵ,𝒬ϵ+1)→(M′,{−,−}ϵ′,𝒬ϵ+1′)\big(M,\{-,-\}_{\epsilon},\mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon+1}\big)\rightarrow\big(M^{\prime},\{-,-\}^{\prime}_{\epsilon},\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}_{\epsilon+1}\big) consists of a smooth map φ:M→M′\varphi:M\rightarrow M^{\prime} that satisfies

φ∗​({f,g}ϵ′)={φ∗​f,φ∗​g}ϵ,φ∗​𝒬′=𝒬,\varphi^{*}\big(\{f,g\}^{\prime}_{\epsilon}\big)=\{\varphi^{*}f,\varphi^{*}g\}_{\epsilon}\,,\qquad\varphi^{*}\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}=\mathcal{Q}\,,

for all f,g∈C∞​(M′)f,g\in C^{\infty}(M^{\prime}). Directly we have

φ∗​(Q′​(f))=φ∗​({𝒬ϵ+1′,f}ϵ′)={φ∗​𝒬ϵ+1′,φ∗​f}ϵ={𝒬​φ∗f}ϵ=Q⁡(φ∗​f).\varphi^{*}\big(Q^{\prime}(f)\big)=\varphi^{*}\big(\{\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}_{\epsilon+1},f\}^{\prime}_{\epsilon}\big)=\{\varphi^{*}\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}_{\epsilon+1},\varphi^{*}f\}_{\epsilon}=\{\mathcal{Q}\varphi*f\}_{\epsilon}=Q(\varphi^{*}f)\,.

Thus, morphism of gauge systems induce morphisms between the respective derived associative algebras.

Example 2.6.

Given a Q-manifold (M,Q)(M,Q), there is an ‘odd anchor’ map 𝖺Q:M→Π​𝖳​M\mathsf{a}_{Q}:M\rightarrow\Pi{{T}}M, given in local coordinates as 𝖺Q∗​(xa,d​xb)=(xa,Qb​(x))\mathsf{a}^{*}_{Q}\big(x^{a},\textnormal{d}x^{b}\big)=\big(x^{a},Q^{b}(x)\big), where the homological vector field is Q=Qa(x)∂aQ=Q^{a}(x)\partial_{a}. The odd tangent bundle is itself a Q-manifold; functions on Π​𝖳​M\Pi{{T}}M are defined as pseudo-differential forms on MM and the homological vector field is the de Rham differential d=dxa∂a\textnormal{d}=\textnormal{d}x^{a}\partial_{a}. Thus, we set Ω∙​(M):=C∞​(Π​𝖳​M)\Omega^{\bullet}(M):=C^{\infty}(\Pi{{T}}M). It can be shown, see [6, Proposition 2.8], that 𝖺Q:(M,Q)→(Π​𝖳​M,d)\mathsf{a}_{Q}:(M,Q)\rightarrow(\Pi{{T}}M,\textnormal{d}) is a Q-morphism, i.e., Q∘𝖺Q∗−𝖺Q∗∘d=0Q\circ\mathsf{a}^{*}_{Q}-\mathsf{a}^{*}_{Q}\circ\textnormal{d}=0. Thus,

𝖺Q∗:(Ω∙(M),⋆d)→(M,⋆Q),\mathsf{a}^{*}_{Q}:\big(\Omega^{\bullet}(M),\star_{\textnormal{d}}\big)\rightarrow\big(M,\star_{Q}\big)\,,

is a morphism of derived associative algebras.

Although 𝒪:SManop→SAlg\mathcal{O}:\textnormal{{SMan}}^{\textrm{op}}\rightarrow\textnormal{{SAlg}} is fully faithful, 𝒪der:QManop→NUSAlg\mathcal{O}_{\textrm{der}}:\textnormal{{QMan}}^{\textrm{op}}\rightarrow\textnormal{{NUSAlg}} fails to be full, i.e., there may be more morphisms as algebras than Q-manifolds. This can easily be argued as the derived product does not have a unit that must be respected if the morphism is to come from a supermanifold morphism.

Proposition 2.3.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold. Then the set of left absorbers of the derived product is identified with the set of Q-closed functions 𝒵⁡(M)\mathcal{Z}(M).

Proof.

We require f⋆g=(−1)f~​Q​(f)​g=0f\star g=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q(f)g=0 for all g∈C∞​(M)g\in C^{\infty}(M). Setting g=1g=1, we obtain Q⁡(f)=0Q(f)=0. Thus, f∈𝒵⁡(M)f\in\mathcal{Z}(M), as required. ∎

Observation 2.1.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold such that Q≠𝟎Q\neq\bm{0}; then the zero function is a right absorber of the derived product.

Due to nilpotent elements, we cannot conclude that the zero function is a unique absorber. For example, consider ℝ1|1{\mathbb{R}}^{1|1} which we equip with coordinates (x,θ)(x,\theta), and the homological vector field Q=θ∂xQ=\theta\partial_{x}. Then for any f=f0+θ​f1f=f_{0}+\theta\,f_{1} and f=f0+θ​f1f=f_{0}+\theta\,f_{1} we have f⋆g=−θ​f1′​(g0+θ​g1)f\star g=-\theta\,f^{\prime}_{1}(g_{0}+\theta\,g_{1}). As θ2=0\theta^{2}=0, right absorbers are of the form 0+θ​g10+\theta\,g_{1}, where g1g_{1} is an arbitrary (smooth) function of xx. Note that there is no unit element for the derived product, as ⋆\star shifts the Grassmann parity of the functions. Thus, we have no notion of units for the derived product, i.e., there are no invertible functions with respect to the derived product. The adjoining of a unit is discussed in Subsection 2.6.

We may have functions (at least locally) such that f⋆g=1f\star g=1. For example, on ℝp|q{\mathbb{R}}^{p|q} with coordinates (xa,θα)(x^{a},\theta^{\alpha}) equipped with the homological vector field Q:=∂θ1Q:=\partial_{\theta^{1}}, the functions f=−θ1f=-\theta^{1} and g=1g=1 satisfy f⋆g=1f\star g=1. However, the unit function is not the unit/identity element of the derived associative product. Given the odd nature of the derived product, we make the following definition.

Definition 2.2.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold. The derived commutator of f,g∈C∞​(M)f,g\in C^{\infty}(M) is defined as

[f,g]⋆:=f⋆g−(−1)(f~+1)​(g~+1)​g⋆f=(−1)f~​Q​(f​g).[f,g]_{\star}:=f\star g-(-1)^{(\widetilde{f}+1)(\widetilde{g}+1)}\,g\star f=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q(fg)\,.

Two functions ff and gg are said to derived commute if [f,g]⋆=0[f,g]_{\star}=0.

Observation 2.2.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold, then functions ff and g∈C∞​(M)g\in C^{\infty}(M) derived commute, i.e., [f,g]⋆=0[f,g]_{\star}=0, if and only if f​g∈𝒵⁡(M)fg\in\mathcal{Z}(M).

Proposition 2.4.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold such that Q≠𝟎Q\neq\mathbf{0}. Then 𝒵⁡(M,Q):=ker⁡(Q)\mathcal{Z}(M,Q):=\ker(Q) and ℬ⁡(M,Q):=Im⁡(Q)\mathcal{B}(M,Q):=\mathrm{Im}(Q) are two-sided ideals of the derived associative algebra of (M,Q)(M,Q).

Proof.

Assume that f∈𝒵⁡(M,Q)f\in\mathcal{Z}(M,Q) and that g∈C∞​(M)g\in C^{\infty}(M). Then f⋆g=0∈𝒵⁡(M,Q)f\star g=0\in\mathcal{Z}(M,Q) as Q-closed functions are left absorbers (see Proposition 2.3). Similarly, g⋆f=±Q⁡(g)​f=±Q⁡(g​f)∈𝒵⁡(M,Q)g\star f=\pm Q(g)f=\pm Q(gf)\in\mathcal{Z}(M,Q) as ff is Q-closed. Thus, 𝒵⁡(M,Q)\mathcal{Z}(M,Q) is a two-sided ideal of the derived associative algebra. The same reasoning establishes that ℬ⁡(M,Q)⊂𝒵⁡(M,Q)\mathcal{B}(M,Q)\subset\mathcal{Z}(M,Q) is also a two-sided ideal. ∎

We may have non-trivial idempotents, i.e., functions such that f⋆f=ff\star f=f. Note we require f~=1\widetilde{f}=1 (or equivalently f¯=0\overline{f}=0). For example, on ℝ0|1{\mathbb{R}}^{0|1} with a single coordinate θ\theta and Q=∂θQ=\partial_{\theta}, f=−θf=-\theta is an idempotent. As the commutator bracket in an associative algebra forms a Poisson algebra, the following result is naturally expected.

Proposition 2.5.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold. Then the derived commutator satisfies

  1. i)

    [f,[g,h]⋆]⋆=[[f,g]⋆,h]⋆+(−1)(f~+1)​(g~+1)​[g,[f,h]⋆]⋆[f,[g,h]_{\star}]_{\star}=[[f,g]_{\star},h]_{\star}+(-1)^{(\widetilde{f}+1)(\widetilde{g}+1)}\,[g,[f,h]_{\star}]_{\star};

  2. ii)

    [f,g⋆h]⋆=[f,g]⋆⋆h+(−1)(f~+1)​(g~+1)​g⋆[f,h]⋆[f,g\star h]_{\star}=[f,g]_{\star}\star h+(-1)^{(\widetilde{f}+1)(\widetilde{g}+1)}\,g\star[f,h]_{\star},

for all f,gf,g and h∈C∞​(M)h\in C^{\infty}(M).

Proof.

We observe that the derived associative algebra is a standard associative algebra with respect to the shifted grading defined by f¯=f~+1\overline{f}=\widetilde{f}+1. It is a standard result that the commutator bracket on an associative algebra is a Poisson bracket. Thus, the above properties hold. ∎

Proposition 2.5 can also be directly proved from the definition of the derived commutator and Q2=0Q^{2}=0. We will refer to (C∞​(M),+,⋆,[−,−]⋆)(C^{\infty}(M),+,\star,[-,-]_{\star}) as the derived Poisson algebra of (M,Q)(M,Q), noting that we have a standard Poisson algebra using the shifted grading. It is important to note that [f,g]⋆∈𝒵⁡(M)[f,g]_{\star}\in\mathcal{Z}(M), and so is a left absorber via Proposition 2.3, i.e., [f,g]⋆⋆h=0[f,g]_{\star}\star h=0 for all f,gf,g and h∈C∞​(M)h\in C^{\infty}(M).

Using the shifted grading, we have a standard Lie algebra; that is, the Jacobi identity is simply

(2.2) [f,[g,h]⋆]⋆=[[f,g]⋆,h]⋆+(−1)f¯​g¯​[g,[f,h]⋆]⋆.[f,[g,h]_{\star}]_{\star}=[[f,g]_{\star},h]_{\star}+(-1)^{\overline{f}\,\overline{g}}\,[g,[f,h]_{\star}]_{\star}\,.

2.2. Infinitesimal Symmetries and Derived Derivations

The definition of an infinitesimal symmetry of a Q-manifold is the following.

Definition 2.3.

An infinitesimal symmetry of a Q-manifold (M,Q)(M,Q) is a vector field X∈𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(M)X\in{Vect}(M) such that ℒX​Q=[X,Q]=0\mathcal{L}_{X}Q=[X,Q]=0.

The ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-vector space of infinitesimal symmetries forms a Lie algebra with respect to the Lie bracket of vector fields. Geometrically, the infinitesimal change of QQ in the ‘direction’ XX is zero whenever we have an infinitesimal symmetry. We will denote the Lie algebra of infinitesimal symmetries as (Sym⁡(M,Q),[−,−])\big(\mathrm{Sym}(M,Q),[-,-]\big).

Example 2.7.

Let f∈𝒵⁡(M,Q)f\in\mathcal{Z}(M,Q), i.e., Q⁡(f)=0Q(f)=0. Then X:=f​QX:=f\,Q is an infinitesimal symmetry. To see this, we observe that

[X,Q]=[f​Q,Q]=(−1)f~​[Q,f​Q]=(−1)f~​Q​(f)​Q+f⁡[Q,Q]=0.[X,Q]=[f\,Q,Q]=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,[Q,f\,Q]=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q(f)\,Q+f\,[Q,Q]=0\,.
Example 2.8.

Let NN be a pure even manifold. Then (Π​𝖳​N,d)(\Pi{{T}}N,\textnormal{d}) is a Q-manifold. Let u∈𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(N)u\in{Vect}(N) be an arbitrary vector field. Then the Lie derivative ℒu\mathcal{L}_{u} is a vector field on Π​𝖳​N\Pi{{T}}N. As [ℒu,d]=0[\mathcal{L}_{u},\textnormal{d}]=0, ℒu\mathcal{L}_{u} is an infinitesimal symmetry. Moreover, [ℒu,ℒv]=ℒ[u,v][\mathcal{L}_{u},\mathcal{L}_{v}]=\mathcal{L}_{[u,v]}.

Infinitesimal symmetries preserve the odd (generally singular) distribution 𝒟Q:=Span⁡{Q}\mathcal{D}_{Q}:=\Span\{Q\}. The notion of a derivation of the derived associative algebra is clear.

Definition 2.4.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold. A derived derivation is an ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-linear map D:C∞​(M)→C∞​(M)D:C^{\infty}(M)\rightarrow C^{\infty}(M) that satisfies the shifted Leibniz rule

D⁡(f⋆g)=D⁡(f)⋆g+(−1)D¯​f¯​f⋆D⁡(g),D(f\star g)=D(f)\star g+(-1)^{\overline{D}\,\overline{f}}\,f\star D(g)\,,

for all f,g∈C∞​(M)f,g\in C^{\infty}(M). The ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-vector space of derived derivations we denote as Der⋆⁡(M)\Der_{\star}(M).

Note that as the derived associative algebra of (M,Q)(M,Q) is inherently noncommutative (assuming Q≠𝟎Q\neq\bm{0}), derived derivations do not form a (left or right) module over the algebra. We define the Lie bracket of derived derivations as expected:

(2.3) [D1,D2]⋆:=D1∘D2−(−1)D¯1​D¯2​D2∘D1.[D_{1},D_{2}]_{\star}:=D_{1}\circ D_{2}-(-1)^{\overline{D}_{1}\,\overline{D}_{2}}\,D_{2}\circ D_{1}\,.

Note that we have the standard Lie bracket of derivations with respect to the shifted grading. Thus, we can immediately infer that derived derivations form a Lie algebra. From Proposition 2.5, we have inner derived derivations defined as

(2.4) Df:=[f,−]⋆,D_{f}:=[f,-]_{\star}\,,

for any f∈C∞​(M)f\in C^{\infty}(M). Note that we have Df¯=f~+1=f¯\overline{D_{f}}=\widetilde{f}+1=\overline{f}. A derived derivation is said to be an outer derived derivation if it is not an inner derived derivation. We will denote the space of inner derived derivations as Inn⋆​(M)\textrm{Inn}_{\star}(M). Formally, the outer derived derivations are defined as as Out⋆​(M):=Der⋆⁡(M)/Inn⋆​(M)\textrm{Out}_{\star}(M):=\Der_{\star}(M)/\textrm{Inn}_{\star}(M).

Example 2.9.

On any Q-manifold we have D1​(f):=[1,f]⋆=Q⁡(f)D_{1}(f):=[1,f]_{\star}=Q(f), which is an inner derived derivation.

Observe that for vector fields X∈𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(M)X\in{Vect}(M) we have X¯=X~\overline{X}=\widetilde{X}. To see this, recall that X⁡(f)~=X~+f~\widetilde{X(f)}=\widetilde{X}+\widetilde{f}. This implies that X⁡(f)¯=X~+f~+1\overline{X(f)}=\widetilde{X}+\widetilde{f}+1. On the other hand, X⁡(f)¯=X¯+f¯=X¯+f~+1\overline{X(f)}=\overline{X}+\overline{f}=\overline{X}+\widetilde{f}+1. Thus, X¯=X~\overline{X}=\widetilde{X}.

Proposition 2.6.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold. The Lie algebra of infinitesimal symmetries (Sym⁡(M,Q),[−,−])\big(\mathrm{Sym}(M,Q),[-,-]\big) naturally embeds into the Lie algebra of derived derivations (Der⋆⁡(M),[−,−]⋆)\big(\Der_{\star}(M),[-,-]_{\star}\big).

Proof.

First [X,Q]=0[X,Q]=0 implies that X∘Q=(−1)X~​Q∘XX\circ Q=(-1)^{\widetilde{X}}\,Q\circ X. Then directly we have

X⁡(f⋆g)\displaystyle X(f\star g) =X⁡((−1)f~​Q​(f)​g)=(−1)f~​X​Q​(f)​g+(−1)f~+X~​f~+X~​Q​(f)​X​(g)\displaystyle=X\big((-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q(f)g\big)=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,XQ(f)g+(-1)^{\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{X}\,\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{X}}\,Q(f)X(g)
=(−1)f~+X~​Q​X​(f)​g+(−1)f~+X~​f~+X~​Q​(f)​X​(g)=X⁡(f)⋆g+(−1)X~​(f~+1)​f⋆X⁡(g)\displaystyle=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{X}}\,QX(f)g+(-1)^{\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{X}\,\widetilde{f}+\widetilde{X}}\,Q(f)X(g)=X(f)\star g+(-1)^{\widetilde{X}(\widetilde{f}+1)}\,f\star X(g)
=X⁡(f)⋆g+(−1)X¯​f¯​f⋆X⁡(g).\displaystyle=X(f)\star g+(-1)^{\overline{X}\,\overline{f}}\,f\star X(g)\,.

Thus, there is an inclusion of ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-vector spaces Sym⁡(M,Q)↪Der⋆⁡(M)\mathrm{Sym}(M,Q)\hookrightarrow\Der_{\star}(M). We then observe that, by employing the shifted grading, the Lie bracket [−,−]⋆[-,-]_{\star} restricted to the image of the inclusion is precisely the standard Lie bracket of vector fields. Thus, the inclusion is at the level of Lie algebras. ∎

Example 2.10.

Let NN be a smooth manifold; then differential forms on NN are understood as functions on M:=Π​𝖳​NM:=\Pi{{T}}N, and the de Rham differential is understood as a homological vector field. Thus, Ω∙​(N)≅C∞​(Π​𝖳​N)\Omega^{\bullet}(N)\cong C^{\infty}(\Pi{{T}}N). The shifted product is α⋆β=(−1)α~​d​α∧β\alpha\star\beta=(-1)^{\widetilde{\alpha}}\,\textnormal{d}\alpha\wedge\beta. We know (see [23, Chapter II, Section 8]) that all derivations of Ω∙​(N)\Omega^{\bullet}(N) are of the from ℒK=[d,iK]\mathcal{L}_{K}=[\textnormal{d},i_{K}], where K∈Ω∙​(N,𝖳​N)K\in\Omega^{\bullet}(N,{{T}}N) is a vector-valued differential form. Thus, Fröclicher–Nijenhuis operators of the form ℒK\mathcal{L}_{K} are naturally embedded in the Lie algebra of derived derivations.

2.3. Derived Left Modules

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a left C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M)-module (with the standard product of functions). We will write the action as juxtaposition. We will not insist that the module is locally free, though that is the natural case in supergeometry.

Definition 2.5.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold with Q≠𝟎Q\neq\bm{0}, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a left C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M)-module. The derived external composition is the map C∞​(M)×ℳ→ℳC^{\infty}(M)\times\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M} given by

(f,u)↦f⋆u:=(−1)f~​Q​(f)​u.(f,u)\mapsto f\star u:=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q(f)u\,.

Using the shifted grading, we set u¯=u~\overline{u}=\widetilde{u}, and effectively only shift the grading of the functions. In doing so, f⋆u¯=f¯+u¯\overline{f\star u}=\overline{f}+\overline{u}.

Proposition 2.7.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold with Q≠𝟎Q\neq\bm{0}, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a left C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M)-module. The derived external composition is an action of the derived associative algebra on ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Proof.

A direct calculation establishes the proposition. Explicitly,

(f⋆g)⋆u=(−1)g~+1​Q​(Q⁡(f)​g)​u=(−1)g~+f~​Q​(f)​Q​(g)​u=f⋆(g⋆u).(f\star g)\star u=(-1)^{\widetilde{g}+1}\,Q\big(Q(f)g\big)u=(-1)^{\widetilde{g}+\widetilde{f}}\,Q(f)Q(g)u=f\star(g\star u)\,.

∎

Note that as the derived product has no unit element, it is meaningless to speak of (locally) free modules with respect to the derived external composition.

Observation 2.3.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold with Q≠𝟎Q\neq\bm{0}, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a left C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M)-module. Then 𝒵⁡(M,Q):=ker⁡(Q)\mathcal{Z}(M,Q):=\ker(Q) are the annihilators of the derived external composition.

Example 2.11.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold and consider 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(M){Vect}(M). The derived external composition is f⋆X:=(−1)f~​Q​(f)​Xf\star X:=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q(f)X. Now suppose we have an affine connection ∇\nabla; then

∇Q(f⋆X)=(−1)f~​∇Q(Q⁡(f)​X)=(−1)f¯​f⋆∇QX.\nabla_{Q}\big(f\star X\big)=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,\nabla_{Q}\big(Q(f)X\big)=(-1)^{\overline{f}}\,f\star\nabla_{Q}X\,.

That is, ∇Q\nabla_{Q} is a derived linear operator on vector fields.

2.4. Double Q-manifolds and Compatible Derived Associative Algebras

The definition of a double Q-manifold is a supermanifold with a pair of compatible homological vector fields. More formally, we have the following.

Definition 2.6.

A double Q-manifold is a triple (M,Q1,Q2)(M,Q_{1},Q_{2}), where each (M,Qi)(M,Q_{i}) (i=1,2i=1,2) are Q-manifolds and [Q1,Q2]=0[Q_{1},Q_{2}]=0.

Within physics, we may interpret, modulo (multi-)weight, the pair of homological vector fields within the BRST-anti-BRST formalism as the BRST-differential and the anti-BRST-differential (see, for example, [4]).

On any double Q-manifold we have a pair of derived associative algebras defined in the obvious way, i.e.,

(2.5) f⋆ig:=(−1)f~​Qi​(f)​g,f\star_{i}g:=(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q_{i}(f)g\,,

with i=1,2i=1,2.

Recall that a pair of associative algebras on the same vector space is said to be a pair of compatible associative algebras if any linear combination of their binary products defines another associative product.

Proposition 2.8.

Let (M,Q1,Q2)(M,Q_{1},Q_{2}) be a double Q-manifold. The pair of associated derived associative algebras is a pair of compatible (derived) associative algebras.

Proof.

We define f⋆g:=a⁡(f⋆1g)+b⁡(f⋆2g)f\star g:=a\,(f\star_{1}g)+b\,(f\star_{2}g), with aa and b∈ℝb\in{\mathbb{R}} arbitrary. Clearly, this is just the derived multiplication defined by

Q:=a​Q1+b​Q2.Q:=a\,Q_{1}+b\,Q_{2}\,.

The condition [Q1,Q2]=0[Q_{1},Q_{2}]=0 ensures that QQ is a homological vector field, and so ⋆\star defines a derived associative multiplication. Thus, the pair of derived associative algebras is a pair of compatible associative algebras. ∎

One can directly deduce from the definitions the standard compatibility condition

(f⋆1g)⋆2h+(f⋆2g)⋆1h=f⋆1(g⋆2h)+f⋆2(g⋆1h).(f\star_{1}g)\star_{2}h+(f\star_{2}g)\star_{1}h=f\star_{1}(g\star_{2}h)+f\star_{2}(g\star_{1}h)\,.
Example 2.12.

Any Q-manifold (M,Q)(M,Q) may be considered as a double Q-manifold by taking the second homological vector field to be the zero vector field.

Example 2.13.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold. Pseudo-differential forms on MM are understood as functions on Π​𝖳​M\Pi{{T}}M, which itself is canonically a Q-manifold with the homological vector field being identified with the de Rham differential d. The action of QQ may be lifted to act on pseudo-differential forms via the Lie derivative ℒQ:=[d,iQ]\mathcal{L}_{Q}:=[\textnormal{d},i_{Q}], which is recognised as a homological vector field. Cartan’s formula informs us that [d,ℒQ]=0[\textnormal{d},\mathcal{L}_{Q}]=0, and so (Π​𝖳​M,d,ℒQ)(\Pi{{T}}M,\textnormal{d},\mathcal{L}_{Q}) is a double Q-manifold. Thus, the pair of derived associative algebras associated with the de Rham and the Lie derivative with respect to QQ are compatible associative algebras.

Example 2.14.

Following Voronov [46], a double vector bundle DD is a double Lie algebroid, in the sense of Mackenzie [32], if the total parity reversed double vector bundle Π2​D\Pi^{2}D is a double Q-manifold, where the homological vector fields Q(0,1)Q_{(0,1)} and Q(1,0)Q_{(1,0)} are of bi-weight (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0), respectively. Neglecting the bi-weight, the pair of derived associative algebras associated with the homological vector fields are compatible associative algebras.

The results of this subsection directly generalise to nn-tuple Q-manifolds, i,e., supermanifolds equipped with nn homological vector fields that pairwise commute. For example, nn-fold Lie algebroids can be formulated this way; see Voronov [46].

2.5. Derived Associative Algebras of Q-groups

The definition we employ for a Q-group (see Mehta [36]) is the following.

Definition 2.7.

A Q-group (G,Q)(G,Q) is a group object in the category of Q-manifolds.

For group objects in a category, see Mac Lane [33, Chapter III.6] and for Lie supergroups in particular, see [9, Chapter 7]. To spell a Q-group out, we first equip G×GG\times G with the homological vector field Q(2):=Q⊗𝗂𝖽+𝗂𝖽⊗QQ^{(2)}:=Q\otimes\mathsf{id}+\mathsf{id}\otimes Q, and ℝ0|0{\mathbb{R}}^{0|0} with the zero homological vector field 𝟎\mathbf{0}. The structure maps of the Lie supergroup

μ:G×G→G,i:G→G,e:ℝ0|0→G,\mu:G\times G\rightarrow G\,,\qquad i:G\rightarrow G\,,\qquad e:{\mathbb{R}}^{0|0}\rightarrow G\,,

referred to as the multiplication, inverse, and unit maps, respectively, must be morphisms of Q-manifolds. We thus have the compatibility conditions

(2.6a) Q(2)∘μ∗=μ∗∘Q,\displaystyle Q^{(2)}\circ\mu^{*}=\mu^{*}\circ Q\,,
(2.6b) Q∘i∗=i∗∘Q,\displaystyle Q\circ i^{*}=i^{*}\circ Q\,,
(2.6c) e∗∘Q=𝟎.\displaystyle e^{*}\circ Q=\mathbf{0}\,.

Just as in the classical case for multiplicative vector fields on a Lie group, it can be shown that (2.6a) implies both (2.6b) and (2.6c) (see Jubin et al. [26, Proposition 2.20]). Thus, we will refer to QQ as a multiplicative homological vector field.

Example 2.15.

Any Lie supergroup GG may be equipped with the zero homological vector field 𝟎\mathbf{0}; then evidently (G,𝟎)(G,\mathbf{0}) is a Q-group.

Proposition 2.9.

Let (G,Q)(G,Q) be a Q-group. Then the following are morphisms of derived associative algebras:

  1. i)

    μ∗:(C∞(G),⋆Q)→(C∞(G×G),⋆Q(2))\mu^{*}:\big(C^{\infty}(G),\star_{Q}\big)\rightarrow\big(C^{\infty}(G\times G),\star_{Q^{(2)}}\big) ;

  2. ii)

    i∗:(C∞(G),⋆Q)→(C∞(G),⋆Q)i^{*}:\big(C^{\infty}(G),\star_{Q}\big)\rightarrow\big(C^{\infty}(G),\star_{Q}\big) ;

  3. iii)

    e∗:(C∞(G),⋆Q)→(ℝ,⋆𝟎)e^{*}:\big(C^{\infty}(G),\star_{Q}\big)\rightarrow\big({\mathbb{R}},\star_{\bm{0}}\big) .

Proof.

This follows directly from the fact that QQ is a multiplicative homological vector field and Proposition 2.2, which states that morphisms of Q-manifolds induce morphisms between their respective derived associative algebras. ∎

Example 2.16.

Consider supertranslation group ℝ1|1{\mathbb{R}}^{1|1} which we equip with coordinates (x,θ)(x,\theta). The multiplication is given by

μ∗​x=x1+x2+θ1​θ2,μ∗​θ=θ1+θ2.\mu^{*}x=x_{1}+x_{2}+\theta_{1}\theta_{2}\,,\qquad\mu^{*}\theta=\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\,.

The reader can quickly deduce the identity and inverse maps. The multiplicative homological vector field we claim is Q=θ∂xQ=\theta\partial_{x}. Note that the only non-zero derived product of the coordinates is x⋆x=θ​xx\star x=\theta x.

Checking multiplicity explicitly,

μ∗​(Q⁡(x))=μ∗​θ=θ1+θ2\displaystyle\mu^{*}\big(Q(x)\big)=\mu^{*}\theta=\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\, Q(2)(μ∗x)=(θ1∂x1+θ2∂x2)(x1+x2+θ1θ2)=θ1+θ2,\displaystyle Q^{(2)}(\mu^{*}x)=(\theta_{1}\partial_{x_{1}}+\theta_{2}\partial_{x_{2}})(x_{1}+x_{2}+\theta_{1}\theta_{2})=\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\,,
μ∗​(Q⁡(θ))=μ∗​0=0,\displaystyle\mu^{*}\big(Q(\theta)\big)=\mu^{*}0=0\,, Q(2)(μ∗θ)=(θ1∂x1+θ2∂x2)(θ1+θ2)=0.\displaystyle Q^{(2)}(\mu^{*}\theta)=(\theta_{1}\partial_{x_{1}}+\theta_{2}\partial_{x_{2}})(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2})=0\,.

Thus QQ is indeed a multiplicative homological vector field. It is easy to see that i∗​x=−xi^{*}x=-x, i∗​θ=−θi^{*}\theta=-\theta, and e∗​x=0e^{*}x=0 and e∗​θ=0e^{*}\theta=0.

To check that μ∗\mu^{*} is a morphism of derived associative algebras, we first calculate the following.

μ∗​(x⋆x)=μ∗​(θ​x)=μ∗​θ​μ∗​x=(θ1+θ2)​(x1+x2+θ1​θ2)=θ1​x1+θ1​x2+θ2​x1+θ2​x2.\mu^{*}(x\star x)=\mu^{*}(\theta x)=\mu^{*}\theta\,\mu^{*}x=(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2})(x_{1}+x_{2}+\theta_{1}\theta_{2})=\theta_{1}x_{1}+\theta_{1}x_{2}+\theta_{2}x_{1}+\theta_{2}x_{2}\,.

Next observe that Q(2)​(μ∗​x)=θ1+θ2Q^{(2)}(\mu^{*}x)=\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}, where hence,

μ∗​x⋆μ∗​x=(θ1+θ2)​(x1+x2+θ1​θ2)=θ1​x1+θ1​x2+θ2​x1+θ2​x2.\mu^{*}x\star\mu^{*}x=(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2})(x_{1}+x_{2}+\theta_{1}\theta_{2})=\theta_{1}x_{1}+\theta_{1}x_{2}+\theta_{2}x_{1}+\theta_{2}x_{2}\,.

Thus, as expected, μ∗​(x⋆x)=μ∗​x⋆μ∗​x\mu^{*}(x\star x)=\mu^{*}x\star\mu^{*}x.

It is not the case that (C∞(G×G),⋆Q(2))≅(C∞(M),⋆Q)⊗^(C∞(G),⋆Q)\big(C^{\infty}(G\times G),\star_{Q^{(}2)}\big)\cong\big(C^{\infty}(M),\star_{Q}\big)\,\widehat{\otimes}\,\big(C^{\infty}(G),\star_{Q}\big) as associative (shifted) superalgebras. While the category Qman is a Cartesian monoidal category, this does not imply that the derived product is compatible with the (completed) tensor product. We will further comment on this in Section 4.

2.6. Adjoining a Unit Element

The derived associative algebra of a Q-manifold is non-unital. By employing the shifted grading, the standard method of adjoining a unit, also known as the Dorroh extension, can be applied (see [13]). The (minimal) unitalisation of the derived associative algebra is defined as follows. First, the (nuclear Fréchet) super vector space is

(2.7) C∞​(M)+:=C∞​(M)⊕ℝ∋(f,a).C^{\infty}(M)^{+}:=C^{\infty}(M)\oplus{\mathbb{R}}\ni(f,a)\,.

Using the shifted grading, we define a¯=0\overline{a}=0 for all a∈ℝa\in{\mathbb{R}}. This then implies we have

(f,a)∈C0∞​(M)+,if​f¯=0,\displaystyle(f,a)\in C^{\infty}_{0}(M)^{+}~~,\textnormal{if}~\overline{f}=0\,,
(f,0)∈C1∞​(M)+,if​f¯=1,\displaystyle(f,0)\in C^{\infty}_{1}(M)^{+}~~,\textnormal{if}~\overline{f}=1\,,

The derived product is modified as

(2.8) (f,a)⋆(g,b):=(f⋆g+a​g+b​f,a​b).(f,a)\star(g,b):=(f\star g+a\,g+b\,f\,,ab)\,.

Evidently, the unit element is given by e:=(0,1)e:=(0,1). The resulting algebra is a unital associative noncommutative superalgebra. We stress that the unitalisation of the derived associative algebra is not a derived associative algebra of a Q-manifold. For instance, we cannot have a unit element for a derived product. Morphisms of Q-manifolds extend to the unitalisation as φ+​(f,a):=(φ∗​f,a)\varphi^{+}(f,a):=(\varphi^{*}f,a).

In short, we have the composition of functors that take a Q-manifold and produce a unital nuclear Fréchet superalgebra

(M,Q)→(C∞​(M),⋆)→(C∞​(M)+,⋆).(M,Q)\rightarrow(C^{\infty}(M),\star)\rightarrow(C^{\infty}(M)^{+},\star)\,.

We will further comment on the unitalisation in Section 4 during the concluding remarks.

3. Derived Cyclic Cohomology

3.1. The Modular Class and Shifted Graded Traces

Recall that the modular class of a Q-manifold is the obstruction to the existence of a Q-invariant Berezin volume, see [6, 7] for a review. A Q-manifold is said to be unimodular if the modular class vanishes, which by definition means that we can find Berezin volumes 𝝆\rho such that ℒQ​𝝆=0\mathcal{L}_{Q}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$}=0. Note that although the modular class requires a choice of Berezin volume to define, it is independent of this choice and has a cohomological understanding. For applications of modular classes of Q-manifolds in the theory of Lie algebroids, the reader may consult Grabowski [15, 16]. We remark that within the BV-formalism, the vanishing of the modular class implies that there is no ‘one-loop anomaly’ in the corresponding semiclassical quantum theory, see [6, Remark 4.7] and/or [30, Section 6.1], for example.

Proposition 3.1.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a unimodular Q-manifold that is superoriented55 5 By a superoriented supermanifold we mean a supermanifold whose reduced manifold is orientable and an orientation has been chosen, and which possesses an atlas where the standard Jacobian of the even coordinates and the Berezinian of the coordinate transformations are strictly positive. For details of orientations of supermanifolds see Shander [40]. and compact. Then the Berezin integral with respect to a Q-invariant Berezin volume acts as a shifted graded trace on the derived associative algebra.

Proof.

Starting with ∫MℒQ​(ρ​f)=∫M(ℒQ​𝝆)​f+∫M𝝆​Q​(f)\int_{M}\mathcal{L}_{Q}(\rho\,f)=\int_{M}(\mathcal{L}_{Q}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$})\,f+\int_{M}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$}\,Q(f), we observe that if (M,Q)(M,Q) is unimodular and we pick the Q-invariant Berezin volume, this reduces to

∫M𝝆​Q​(f)=0,\int_{M}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$}\,Q(f)=0\,,

where we have used the fact that MM is compact. We then consider f↦(−1)f~​f​gf\mapsto(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,fg, which produces

∫M𝝆​(−1)f~​Q​(f​g)=∫M𝝆​[f,g]⋆=0.\int_{M}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$}\,(-1)^{\widetilde{f}}\,Q(fg)=\int_{M}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$}\,[f,g]_{\star}=0\,.

This is equivalent to ∫M𝝆​f⋆g=∫M𝝆​(−1)f¯​g¯​g⋆f\int_{M}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$}\,f\star g=\int_{M}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$}\,(-1)^{\overline{f}\,\overline{g}}\,g\star f, and hence the integral acts as a shifted graded trace. ∎

Example 3.1.

Let NN be a compact and oriented manifold; then (Π​𝖳​N,d)(\Pi{{T}}N,\textnormal{d}) is a Q-manifold. The canonical Berezin volume (locally this is just the coordinate Berezin volume) is invariant under the de Rham differential. Thus, Π​𝖳​N\Pi{{T}}N is unimodular. Then τ⁡(α):=∫Π​𝖳​N𝝆​α=∫Nαtop\tau(\alpha):=\int_{\Pi{{T}}N}\mbox{\boldmath$\rho$}\,\alpha=\int_{N}\alpha^{\textrm{top}} is a shifted trace over the derived associative algebra given by α⋆β=(−1)α~​d​α∧β\alpha\star\beta=(-1)^{\widetilde{\alpha}}\,\textnormal{d}\alpha\wedge\beta.

As we have established that the Berezin integral can act as a shifted trace, the question of a derived version of Connes’ cyclic cohomology arises.

3.2. Derived Cyclic Cohomology of Q-manifolds

In this subsection, we apply cyclic cohomology to Q-manifolds via the derived associative algebra. Recall that cyclic cohomology was developed by Connes [10] and acts as a generalisation of de Rham cohomology to associative algebras. For a very accessible introduction, the reader may consult Connes [11, Chapter 3], Khalkhali [21], or Weibel [47, Chapter 9]. Kastler [20, Chapter 3] developed Hochschild and cyclic cohomology for ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-graded associative algebras. Thus, by employing the shifted grading to the derived product, we may freely employ Kastler’s constructions and results with minimal amendment.

Let NFSVec be the category of nuclear Fréchet super vector spaces (see Carmeli et al. [9, C.2.]). By definition, morphisms in this category are continuous linear maps. We define nn-cochains as elements of

Cn​(M,Q):=𝖧𝗈𝗆¯NFSVec​(C∞​(M)⊗^n+1,ℝ).C^{n}(M,Q):=\mbox{$\underline{{Hom}}$}_{\textnormal{{NFSVec}}}\big(C^{\infty}(M)^{\widehat{\otimes}^{n+1}},{\mathbb{R}}\big)\,.

Note that C∞​(M):=𝒪M​(|M|)C^{\infty}(M):=\mathcal{O}_{M}(|M|) is a nuclear Fréchet algebra (see [9, Chapter 4.5]). Thus, the projective topology is used to construct the completed tensor product in the definition of nn-cochains. Via Grothendieck’s fundamental theorem of nuclear spaces, other ‘reasonable’ topologies can also be used, such as the injective topology; however, all such completed tensor products coincide (see [41, Chapter 50]).

In differential geometry, the space of distributions, understood as dual objects to functions, is defined using functions with compact support. On a compact (super)manifold there is, of course, no difference between C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M) and Cc∞​(M)C^{\infty}_{c}(M). Note that, for non-compact Q-manifolds, we may consider the derived associative algebra of compactly supported functions (Cc∞​(M),⋆)(C^{\infty}_{c}(M),\star). The complication in doing so is that the underlying vector space is an LF-space, i.e., a strict inductive limit of Fréchet spaces, rather than a Fréchet space itself (see [41, Chapter 13]). While it remains a nuclear space, working with completed projective tensor products of LF-spaces is significantly more complicated than the Fréchet case. Thus, to avoid complications with defining nn-cochains (n>0n>0), we will not insist on compactly supported functions in the definition, and in practice will work with compact supermanifolds. It is irrelevant if one considers the standard or shifted grading with the nn-cochains, as long as one is consistent. Conventionally, we will consider the standard Grassmann parity. The shifted grading can then be applied when required in the formulas to keep track of the sign factors. For pure elements we will write ϕn(f0,f1,⋯,fn):=ϕn(f0⊗f1⊗⋯⊗fn)∈Cn(M,Q)\phi^{n}(f_{0},f_{1},\cdots,f_{n}):=\phi^{n}(f_{0}\otimes f_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{n})\in C^{n}(M,Q). In general, a cochain will be inhomogeneous in grading. We view nn-cochains as generalised currents via direct analogy with de Rham currents66 6 See Current, Encyclopedia of Mathematics, http://encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php?title=Current&oldid=56194, (accessed 16/07/2026).

The shifted cyclic permutation operator λ:Cn​(M,Q)⟶Cn​(M,Q)\lambda\,:C^{n}(M,Q)\longrightarrow C^{n}(M,Q) is defined as

(λ​ϕn)​(f0,f1,⋯,fn):=(−1)n+f¯n​(f¯0+⋯+f¯n−1)​ϕn​(fn,f0,⋯,fn−1).(\lambda\phi^{n})(f_{0},f_{1},\cdots,f_{n}):=(-1)^{n+\overline{f}_{n}\,(\overline{f}_{0}+\cdots+\overline{f}_{n-1})}\,\phi^{n}(f_{n},f_{0},\cdots,f_{n-1})\,.

The space of derived cyclic n-cochains Cλn​(M,Q)⊂Cn​(M,Q)C^{n}_{\lambda}(M,Q)\subset C^{n}(M,Q) consists of nn-cochains that are invariant under λ\lambda, i.e., λ​ϕn=ϕn\lambda\phi^{n}=\phi^{n}.

The Hochschild coboundary operator (see [20]) b:Cn​(M,Q)⟶Cn+1​(M,Q)b:C^{n}(M,Q)\longrightarrow C^{n+1}(M,Q) is defined as

(3.1) (b​ϕn)​(f0,f1,⋯,fn+1)\displaystyle(b\phi^{n})(f_{0},f_{1},\cdots,f_{n+1}) :=∑i=0n(−1)iϕn(f0,⋯fi⋆fi+1,⋯,fn+1)\displaystyle:=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^{i}\,\phi^{n}(f_{0},\cdots f_{i}\star f_{i+1},\cdots,f_{n+1})
+(−1)n+1+f¯n+1​(f¯0+⋯+f¯n)​ϕn​(fn+1⋆f0,⋯,fn).\displaystyle+(-1)^{n+1+\overline{f}_{n+1}\,(\overline{f}_{0}+\cdots+\overline{f}_{n})}\,\phi^{n}(f_{n+1}\star f_{0},\cdots,f_{n})\,.

The result b2=0b^{2}=0 may be directly established. Moreover, it can be shown that the space of derived cyclic cochains is invariant under the Hochschild coboundary operator, i.e., b⁡(Cλn​(M,Q))⊂Cλn+1​(M,Q)b\big(C^{n}_{\lambda}(M,Q)\big)\subset C^{n+1}_{\lambda}(M,Q) (see [20]). Note that the Hochschild coboundary operator is itself continuous as it is defined in terms of a continuous linear map and the operations within the derived associative algebra are continuous.

Observation 3.1.

If all fi∈C∞​(M)f_{i}\in C^{\infty}(M) (i=0,⋯,n+1i=0,\cdots,n+1) are Q-exact, i.e., are all in ℬ⁡(M,Q)\mathcal{B}(M,Q), then b​ϕn​(f0,⋯,fn+1)=0b\phi^{n}(f_{0},\cdots,f_{n+1})=0 for any and all ϕn∈Cn​(M,Q)\phi^{n}\in C^{n}(M,Q).

The derived cyclic complex of (M,Q)(M,Q) is the subcomplex of the derived Hochshild complex given by

(3.2) Cλ0​(M,Q)⟶bCλ1​(M,Q)⟶bCλ2​(M,Q)⟶b⋯.C^{0}_{\lambda}(M,Q)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle b}}{{\longrightarrow}}C^{1}_{\lambda}(M,Q)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle b}}{{\longrightarrow}}C^{2}_{\lambda}(M,Q)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle b}}{{\longrightarrow}}\cdots\,.
Definition 3.1.

The cohomology of the derived cyclic complex (3.2) is referred to as the derived cyclic cohomology of the Q-manifold (M,Q)(M,Q), and will be denoted H​Cλn​(M,Q)HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M,Q), n=0,1,2,⋯n=0,1,2,\cdots. A derived cyclic n-cocycle is a bb-closed derived cyclic nn-cochain. The resulting classes in the derived cyclic cohomology we refer to as derived cyclic classes, and we denote them as [ϕn][\phi^{n}].

Example 3.2.

Consider a trivial Q-manifold (M,𝟎)(M,\bm{0}). The derived product is a zero product, i.e., f⋆g=0f\star g=0 for all f,g∈C∞​(M)f,g\in C^{\infty}(M). In turn, the Hochschild coboundary operator bb is a zero map, and so all derived cochains are bb-closed. Thus, H​Cλn​(M,𝟎)≅Cλn​(M,𝟎)HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M,\bm{0})\cong C^{n}_{\lambda}(M,\bm{0}).

Suppose φ:(M1,Q1)→(M2,Q2)\varphi:(M_{1},Q_{1})\rightarrow(M_{2},Q_{2}) is a morphism of Q-manifolds. Recall that Proposition 2.2 established that φ∗:C∞​(M2)→C∞​(M1)\varphi^{*}:C^{\infty}(M_{2})\rightarrow C^{\infty}(M_{1}) is a morphism of the derived associative algebras. The pushforward of a derived nn-cochain φ∗:Cn​(M1,Q1)→Cn​(M2,Q2)\varphi_{*}:C^{n}(M_{1},Q_{1})\rightarrow C^{n}(M_{2},Q_{2}) is defined as

(3.3) (φ∗​ϕn)​(f0,⋯,fn):=ϕn​(φ∗​f0,⋯,φ∗​fn),\big(\varphi_{*}\phi^{n}\big)(f_{0},\cdots,f_{n}):=\phi^{n}(\varphi^{*}f_{0},\cdots,\varphi^{*}f_{n})\,,

where fi∈C∞​(M2)f_{i}\in C^{\infty}(M_{2}). As φ∗\varphi^{*} does not change the parity (shifted or otherwise), we have φ∗​f¯=f¯\overline{\varphi^{*}f}=\overline{f}; thus the pushforward restricts to derived cyclic nn-cochains. That is

φ∗​(Cλn​(M1,Q1))⊆Cλn​(M2,Q2).\varphi_{*}\big(C^{n}_{\lambda}(M_{1},Q_{1})\big)\subseteq C^{n}_{\lambda}(M_{2},Q_{2})\,.

As φ∗\varphi^{*} is a morphism of the derived associative algebras, applying the Hochschild coboundary operator bb to φ∗​ϕn\varphi^{*}\phi^{n}, one can quickly observe that as standard b∘φ∗=φ∗∘bb\circ\varphi_{*}=\varphi_{*}\circ b. Thus, the pushforward φ∗\varphi_{*} is a cochain map between the derived cyclic complexes. This implies that the pushforward descends to the cohomology:

(3.4) H​Cλn​(M1,Q1)⟶H​Cλn​(M2,Q2)\displaystyle HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M_{1},Q_{1})\longrightarrow HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M_{2},Q_{2})
[ϕn]⟼[φ∗​ϕn].\displaystyle[\phi^{n}]\longmapsto[\varphi_{*}\phi^{n}]\,.

Thus, we have established the following.

Theorem 3.1.

The assignments QMan∈(M,Q)↦H​Cλn​(M,Q)∈SVec,\textnormal{{QMan}}\in(M,Q)\mapsto HC_{\lambda}^{n}(M,Q)\in\textnormal{{SVec}}, and 𝖧𝗈𝗆QMan​((M1,Q1),(M2,Q2))∋φ↦φ∗:H​Cλn​(M1,Q1)→H​Cλn​(M2,Q2){Hom}_{\textnormal{{QMan}}}\big((M_{1},Q_{1}),(M_{2},Q_{2})\big)\ni\varphi\mapsto\varphi_{*}:HC_{\lambda}^{n}(M_{1},Q_{1})\rightarrow HC_{\lambda}^{n}(M_{2},Q_{2}) define a covariant functor H​Cλn:QMan→SVecHC^{n}_{\lambda}:\textnormal{{QMan}}\rightarrow\textnormal{{SVec}} (n=0,1,2,⋯n=0,1,2,\cdots).

Note that we usually have the cohomology of a space being a contravariant functor. However, the derived cyclic cohomology is a cohomology theory of the algebra of functions on a Q-manifold, and thus a covariant functor when considered as a cohomology theory of Q-manifolds.

Corollary 3.1.

If the Q-manifolds (M1,Q1)(M_{1},Q_{1}) and (M2,Q2)(M_{2},Q_{2}) are Q-diffeomorphic, i.e., there is an isomorphism in QMan between them, then H​Cλn​(M1,Q1)≅H​Cλn​(M2,Q2)HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M_{1},Q_{1})\cong HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M_{2},Q_{2}), n=0,1,2,⋯n=0,1,2,\cdots. Conversely, if any of the derived cyclic cohomology groups are not isomorphic, then the Q-manifolds cannot be Q-diffeomorphic.

Theorem 3.1 (together with Corollary 3.1) establishes that derived cyclic cohomology is a genuine algebraic invariant of a Q-manifold.

Proposition 3.2.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold and let (Π​𝖳​M,d)(\Pi{{T}}M,\textnormal{d}) be the odd tangent bundle equipped with the de Rham differential. Then there is a canonical morphism

Ψ:H​Cλn​(M,Q)⟶H​Cλn​(Π​𝖳​M,d)\Psi:HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M,Q)\longrightarrow HC^{n}_{\lambda}(\Pi{{T}}M,\textnormal{d})\,

for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

Proof.

The ‘odd anchor’ 𝖺Q:Ω∙​(M)→C∞​(M)\mathsf{a}_{Q}:\Omega^{\bullet}(M)\rightarrow C^{\infty}(M), which is canonical and exists for all Q-manifolds, is a morphism between the respective derived associative algebras (see Example 2.6). Then, via Theorem 3.1, we know such a morphism induces a morphism between the derived cyclic cochains that descends to the derived cyclic cohomology. We then set

Ψ:\displaystyle\Psi: H​Cλn​(M,Q)⟶H​Cλn​(Π​𝖳​M,d)\displaystyle HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M,Q)\longrightarrow HC^{n}_{\lambda}(\Pi{{T}}M,\textnormal{d})
[ϕn]⟼[(𝖺Q)∗​ϕn].\displaystyle[\phi^{n}]\longmapsto[(\mathsf{a}_{Q})_{*}\phi^{n}]\,.

∎

Any representative of a derived cyclic class [ϕn]∈H​Cλn​(M,Q)[\phi^{n}]\in HC^{n}_{\lambda}(M,Q) is of the form ϕn+b​ψn−1\phi^{n}+b\psi^{n-1}, where ψn−1∈Cλn−1​(M,Q)\psi^{n-1}\in C^{n-1}_{\lambda}(M,Q). A 00-cochain, τ:C∞​(M)→ℝ\tau:C^{\infty}(M)\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}, is a shifted graded trace if and only if τ⁡([f,g]⋆)=0\tau([f,g]_{\star})=0 for all ff and g∈C∞​(M)g\in C^{\infty}(M). Lemma 3.1.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold. A 00-cochain τ\tau is a derived cyclic 00-cocycle if and only if τ∘Q=0\tau\circ Q=0.

Thus, as ff arbitrary, we have τ∘Q=0\tau\circ Q=0. ∎

The above examples, while modest in scope, clearly demonstrate that derived cyclic cohomology is quite independent from the standard cohomology of a Q-manifold.

We expect, in general, calculating the derived cyclic cohomology and explicitly presenting cyclic nn-cocycles for Q-manifolds without extra structure to be very difficult. It is important to note that the derived associative algebra is non-unital and so many of the standard methods of calculating cyclic cohomology, for example Connes’ SBI sequence, will not directly apply to derived cyclic cohomology. We will comment on this a little further in our concluding remarks. In Subsection 3.3 we explore the derived cyclic cohomology of the odd line extending Example 3.4. We will present derived cyclic nn-cocycles for regular foliations via their foliation Lie algebroid in Subsection 3.6. Further examples are left open for future work.

3.3. Derived Cyclic Cohomology of the Odd Line

Consider the odd line M=ℝ0|1M={\mathbb{R}}^{0|1}, which we equip with a global coordinate ¸\mathchar 28952\relax, and a canonical homological vector field given by Q=∂¸Q=\partial_{\mathchar 28952\relax}. 3.5. Applications to Lie Algebras: The Relation with Lie Algebra Homology

In this subsection, we will consider a pure even finite dimensional Lie algebra (𝔤,[−,−])(\mathfrak{g},[-,-]). For details of the homology and cohomology of Lie algebras, the reader may consult Weibel [47, Chapter 7]. Let us choose a basis {ea}\{e_{a}\}, such that [ea,eb]=Qa​bc​ec[e_{a},e_{b}]=Q_{ab}^{c}e_{c}. Shifting the parity of the vector space (now considered as a linear supermanifold), we obtain a Q-manifold (Π​𝔤,dC​E)(\Pi\mathfrak{g},\textnormal{d}_{CE}), where, in coordinates,

(3.14) dC​E=12​ηb​ηa​Qa​bc​∂∂ηc,\textnormal{d}_{CE}=\frac{1}{2}\eta^{b}\eta^{a}Q_{ab}^{c}\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta^{c}}\,,

is recognised as the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential. Note C∞​(Π​𝔤)≅Λ∙​𝔤∗C^{\infty}(\Pi\mathfrak{g})\cong\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}^{*}. We remark that dC​E2=0\textnormal{d}_{CE}^{2}=0 is equivalent to the Jacobi identity for the Lie bracket. Borrowing language from physics, the coordinates ηa\eta^{a} are Faddeev–Popov ghosts.

Clearly, we have the derived associative algebra (C∞​(Π​𝔤),⋆)(C^{\infty}(\Pi\mathfrak{g}),\star) associated with any Lie algebra. The derived 00-cochains are

C0​(Π​𝔤,dC​E):=𝖫𝗂𝗇¯​(Λ∙​𝔤∗,ℝ)=(Λ∙​𝔤∗)∗≅Λ∙​𝔤.C^{0}(\Pi\mathfrak{g},\textnormal{d}_{CE}):=\mbox{$\underline{{Lin}}$}\big(\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}^{*},{\mathbb{R}}\big)=\big(\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}^{*}\big)^{*}\cong\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}\,.

Note that the algebra is finite dimensional, and so the completed tensor product coincides with the algebraic tensor product, meaning we lose no generality considering linear maps between the finite-dimensional super vector spaces. Via Lemma 3.1, all derived cyclic 00-cocycles satisfy τ∘dC​E=0\tau\circ\textnormal{d}_{CE}=0. The canonical pairing ⟨−,−⟩\langle-,-\rangle between Λ∙​𝔤\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g} and Λ∙​𝔤∗\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}^{*} allows us to define the Chevalley–Eilenberg boundary operator ∂C​E\partial_{CE} via

(3.15) ⟨τ,dC​E​α⟩=⟨∂C​Eτ,α⟩.\langle\tau,\textnormal{d}_{CE}\alpha\rangle=\langle\partial_{CE}\tau,\alpha\rangle\,.

Then using the canonical isomorphism (Λ∙​𝔤∗)∗≅Λ∙​𝔤\big(\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}^{*}\big)^{*}\cong\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}, we identify derived cyclic 00-cocycles with Lie algebra (homology) cycles. More formally, we have established the following.

Proposition 3.7.

Let (𝔤,[−,−])(\mathfrak{g},[-,-]) be a (pure even) finite dimensional Lie algebra of dimension nn. Then

H​Cλ0​(Π​𝔤,dC​E)≅𝒵∙​(𝔤)=⨁k=0n𝒵k​(𝔤),HC^{0}_{\lambda}(\Pi\mathfrak{g},\textnormal{d}_{CE})\cong\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}(\mathfrak{g})=\bigoplus_{k=0}^{n}\mathcal{Z}_{k}(\mathfrak{g})\,,

where 𝒵k​(𝔤)\mathcal{Z}_{k}(\mathfrak{g}) are the Lie algebra cycle groups, and we assign Grassmann parity of kk (mod 22) to elements of the Lie algebra kk-cycle group.

Example 3.10.

For any abelian Lie algebra (𝔞,[−,−])(\mathfrak{a},[-,-]) of dimension nn, as the Chevalley–Eilenberg boundary operator is the zero map

H​Cλ0​(Π​𝔞,dC​E)≅𝒵∙​(𝔞)=⨁k=0nΛk​𝔞≅ℝ2n−1|2n−1.HC^{0}_{\lambda}(\Pi\mathfrak{a},\textnormal{d}_{CE})\cong\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}(\mathfrak{a})=\bigoplus_{k=0}^{n}\Lambda^{k}\mathfrak{a}\cong{\mathbb{R}}^{2^{n-1}|2^{n-1}}\,.
Example 3.11.

Consider the 33-dimensional Heisenberg algebra 𝔥\mathfrak{h} given by generators {x,y,z}\{x,y,z\} and non-vanishing Lie bracket [x,y]=z[x,y]=z. Note zz is central. Then 𝒵∙​(𝔥)=𝒵0​(𝔥)​⨁𝒵1​(𝔥)​⨁𝒵2​(𝔥)​⨁𝒵3​(𝔥)\mathcal{Z}_{\bullet}(\mathfrak{h})=\mathcal{Z}_{0}(\mathfrak{h})\bigoplus\mathcal{Z}_{1}(\mathfrak{h})\bigoplus\mathcal{Z}_{2}(\mathfrak{h})\bigoplus\mathcal{Z}_{3}(\mathfrak{h}). Observe that 𝒵0​(𝔥)=ℝ\mathcal{Z}_{0}(\mathfrak{h})={\mathbb{R}}, and so 𝒵1​(𝔥)=𝔥\mathcal{Z}_{1}(\mathfrak{h})=\mathfrak{h}. From the algebra we see that ∂C​E(x∧y)=−z\partial_{CE}(x\wedge y)=-z and ∂C​E(x∧z)=∂C​E(y∧z)=0\partial_{CE}(x\wedge z)=\partial_{CE}(y\wedge z)=0. Thus, 𝒵2​(𝔥)=Span⁡(x∧z,y∧z)\mathcal{Z}_{2}(\mathfrak{h})=\Span(x\wedge z,y\wedge z). Finally, ∂C​E(x∧y∧z)=−z∧z=0\partial_{CE}(x\wedge y\wedge z)=-z\wedge z=0, thus 𝒵3​(𝔥)=Span⁡(x∧y∧z)\mathcal{Z}_{3}(\mathfrak{h})=\Span(x\wedge y\wedge z). In total we have

H​Cλ0​(Π​𝔥,dC​E)≅ℝ​⨁Span⁡(x,y,z)​⨁Span⁡(x∧z,y∧z)​⨁Span⁡(x∧y∧z)≅ℝ3|4.HC^{0}_{\lambda}(\Pi\mathfrak{h},\textnormal{d}_{CE})\cong{\mathbb{R}}\bigoplus\Span(x,y,z)\bigoplus\Span(x\wedge z,y\wedge z)\bigoplus\Span(x\wedge y\wedge z)\cong{\mathbb{R}}^{3|4}\,.

While Cλn(Π𝔤,dC​E)⊂(Λ∙𝔤)⊗n+1≅𝖫𝗂𝗇¯((Λ∙𝔤∗)⊗n+1,ℝ)C^{n}_{\lambda}(\Pi\mathfrak{g},\textnormal{d}_{CE})\subset\big(\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}\big)^{\otimes^{n+1}}\cong\mbox{$\underline{{Lin}}$}\big((\Lambda^{\bullet}\mathfrak{g}^{*})^{\otimes^{n+1}},{\mathbb{R}}\big), we do not have a simple generalisation of Proposition 3.7 for n>0n>0 and non-abelian Lie algebras. In particular, for the n>0n>0 case, we have bb-exact cochains to contend with when calculating the derived cyclic cohomology, and this prevents a simple decomposition relating it to the Lie algebra homology.

3.6. Applications to Regular Foliations: Generalised Currents

Let NN be a pure even manifold and let A⊂𝖳​NA\subset{{T}}N be an integrable subbundle defining a regular foliation ℱ={Li}i∈ℐ\mathcal{F}=\{L_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} of NN. This defines the foliation Lie algebroid of the regular foliation. Sections of AA are vector fields tangent to ℱ\mathcal{F}. The Lie bracket is the restriction of the standard Lie bracket of vector fields, and the anchor is the inclusion map (and so it is injective). Moreover, the orbit foliation of the anchor is precisely the foliation ℱ\mathcal{F}. Conversely, any Lie algebroid with an injective anchor map is isomorphic to a foliation Lie algebroid.

The corresponding Q-manifold picture is as follows. The supermanifold is Π​A\Pi A (the parity reversed vector bundle), and so C∞​(Π​A)C^{\infty}(\Pi A) is identified with leaf-wise (pseudo-)differential forms Ω∙​(ℱ)\Omega^{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}). The homological vector field is the restriction of the de Rham differential to the leaves of the foliation, i.e., Q=dℱQ=\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}}. The derived product is then α⋆β:=(−1)α~​dℱ​α∧β\alpha\star\beta:=(-1)^{\widetilde{\alpha}}\,\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}}\alpha\wedge\beta, with α,β∈Ω∙​(ℱ)\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}). The modular class of a foliation Lie algebroid (see Subsection 3.1) is the obstruction to the existence of a global, strictly positive, nowhere-vanishing transverse invariant volume. In classical language, the modular class of a foliation Lie algebroid is known as the Reeb class.

Moving to derived cyclic cohomology of the foliation, the derived nn-cochains are elements of

Cn​(Π​A,dℱ):=𝖧𝗈𝗆¯NFSVec​((Ω∙​(ℱ))⊗^n+1,ℝ).C^{n}(\Pi A,\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}}):=\mbox{$\underline{{Hom}}$}_{\textnormal{{NFSVec}}}\big((\Omega^{\bullet}(\mathcal{F}))^{\widehat{\otimes}^{n+1}},{\mathbb{R}}\big)\,.

Some comments:

  1. i)

    Derived 00-cochains are generalised foliation currents; we recover classical foliation currents when restricting to leaf-wise top-forms with compact support.

  2. ii)

    Derived cyclic 00-cocycles, via Lemma 3.1 (or Proposition 3.3), satisfy τ∘dℱ=0\tau\circ\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}}=0. A foliation current that vanishes on leaf-wise exact forms is a closed foliation current (or a holonomy-invariant transverse current), see Ruelle & Sullivan [37]. Thus, derived cyclic 00-cocycles are generalised closed foliation currents.

  3. iii)

    Derived cyclic nn-cocycles (n≥1n\geq 1) are interpreted as generalised closed foliation multiform currents. Their precise interpretation in terms of classical foliation theory is currently unclear. As far as the author is aware, multilinear functionals of leaf-wise differential forms have not been considered before.

Example 3.12.

Consider the torus T2=S1×S1T^{2}=S^{1}\times S^{1} which we equip with angular coordinates (ϑ,φ)∈[0,2​π)×[0,2​π)(\vartheta,\varphi)\in[0,2\,\pi)\times[0,2\,\pi). The foliation we consider is the horizontal foliation given by φ=constant\varphi=\textrm{constant}. The associated foliation Lie algebroid Π​A\Pi A has adapted coordinates (ϑ,φ,d​ϑ)(\vartheta,\varphi,\textnormal{d}\vartheta). The homological vector field is given by dℱ=dϑ∂ϑ\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}}=\textnormal{d}\vartheta\partial_{\vartheta}. As any leaf-wise (pseudo-)differential form has the structure α=α0​(ϑ,φ)+d​ϑ​α1​(ϑ,φ)\alpha=\alpha_{0}(\vartheta,\varphi)+\textnormal{d}\vartheta\alpha_{1}(\vartheta,\varphi), we observe that α⋆β=d​ϑ​∂ϑα0​(ϑ,φ)​β0​(ϑ,φ)\alpha\star\beta=\textnormal{d}\vartheta\partial_{\vartheta}\alpha_{0}(\vartheta,\varphi)\,\beta_{0}(\vartheta,\varphi) as there are no non-zero leaf-wise 22-forms. We remark this also implies that α⋆β⋆γ=0\alpha\star\beta\star\gamma=0. We will fix an orientation.

Let τ\tau be a derived cyclic 00-cocycle. We have the decomposition τ⁡(α)=τ0​(α0)+τ1​(d​ϑ​α1)\tau(\alpha)=\tau_{0}(\alpha_{0})+\tau_{1}(\textnormal{d}\vartheta\alpha_{1}). Furthermore, we know that τ∘dℱ=0\tau\circ\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}}=0.

  • •

    τ0\tau_{0} is unconstrained as there are no leaf-wise −1-1-forms, i.e., functions are never dℱ\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}}-exact.

  • •

    τ1\tau_{1} must annihilate ϑ\vartheta-derivatives. Via the standard theory of distributions on S1S^{1} (which is obviously compact), we know that any functional that vanishes on exact one-forms must be a multiple of the integral over S1S^{1}. Thus,

    τ1​(d​ϑ​α1)=∫T2d​ϑ​d​φ​μ​(φ)​α1​(ϑ,φ),\tau_{1}(\textnormal{d}\vartheta\alpha_{1})=\int_{T^{2}}\textnormal{d}\vartheta\,\textnormal{d}\varphi\,\mu(\varphi)\,\alpha_{1}(\vartheta,\varphi)\,,

    where μ⁡(φ)\mu(\varphi) is a transverse invariant measure (via [37]). That is, τ1\tau_{1} is a classical Ruelle–Sullivan current.

To construct a derived cyclic 11-cocycle, we set τ0=0\tau_{0}=0 and fix some transverse invariant measure μ⁡(φ)\mu(\varphi). That is, we will set τ\tau to be a classical Ruelle–Sullivan current. We then select a vector field tangent to the leaves X∈𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍ℱ​(T2)X\in{Vect}_{\mathcal{F}}(T^{2}). The leaf-wise Lie derivative is defined as ℒXℱ:=[dℱ,iX]\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X}:=[\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}},i_{X}]. We write X=f(ϑ,φ)∂ϑX=f(\vartheta,\varphi)\partial_{\vartheta}. Note that for γ:=d​ϑ​γ1​(ϑ,φ)\gamma:=\textnormal{d}\vartheta\,\gamma_{1}(\vartheta,\varphi), we have ℒXℱ​γ=d​ϑ​∂ϑ(f​γ1)\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X}\gamma=\textnormal{d}\vartheta\partial_{\vartheta}(f\gamma_{1}). Then, for α=α0+d​ϑ​α1\alpha=\alpha_{0}+\textnormal{d}\vartheta\alpha_{1} we see that

τ⁡(ℒXℱ​α)=∫T2d​ϑ​d​φ​μ​(φ)​∂ϑ(f​α1).\tau\big(\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X}\alpha\big)=\int_{T^{2}}\textnormal{d}\vartheta\textnormal{d}\varphi\,\mu(\varphi)\,\partial_{\vartheta}(f\alpha_{1})\,.

Via the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus applied to the closed loop S1S^{1}, τ⁡(ℒXℱ​α)=0\tau\big(\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X}\alpha\big)=0. Thus, τ\tau is invariant under the leaf-wise Lie derivative. We then define

ϕX1​(α,β):=τ⁡(α⋆ℒXℱ​β)=τ⁡(α0⋆X⁡(β0))=∫T2d​ϑ​d​φ​μ​(φ)​f​(ϑ,φ)​(∂ϑ(α0))​(∂ϑ(β0)).\phi^{1}_{X}(\alpha,\beta):=\tau\big(\alpha\star\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X}\beta\big)=\tau\big(\alpha_{0}\star X(\beta_{0})\big)=\int_{T^{2}}\textnormal{d}\vartheta\textnormal{d}\varphi\,\mu(\varphi)\,f(\vartheta,\varphi)\big(\partial_{\vartheta}(\alpha_{0})\big)\big(\partial_{\vartheta}(\beta_{0})\big)\,.

As the only non-zero components of the functional are related to α0\alpha_{0} and β0\beta_{0}, we will consider ϕX1​(α0,β0)\phi^{1}_{X}(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0}). Note that using the shifted grading α¯0=β¯0=1\overline{\alpha}_{0}=\overline{\beta}_{0}=1. Via inspection, we see that ϕX1​(α0,β0)=ϕX1​(β0,α0)\phi^{1}_{X}(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0})=\phi^{1}_{X}(\beta_{0},\alpha_{0}), and thus ϕX1\phi^{1}_{X} is shifted cyclic.

Checking the action of the Hochschild coboundary operator, we have by definition

(b​ϕX1)​(α,β,γ):=ϕX1​(α⋆β,γ)−ϕX1​(α,β⋆γ)+(−1)γ¯​(α¯+β¯)​ϕX1​(γ⋆α,β).(b\phi^{1}_{X})(\alpha,\beta,\gamma):=\phi^{1}_{X}(\alpha\star\beta,\gamma)-\phi^{1}_{X}(\alpha,\beta\star\gamma)+(-1)^{\overline{\gamma}\,(\overline{\alpha}+\overline{\beta})}\,\phi^{1}_{X}(\gamma\star\alpha,\beta)\,.
