Example 3.12 suggests a method of constructing derived cyclic nn-cocycles for more general regular foliations provided the modular class of the foliation Lie algebroid vanishes. Suppose dimN=d\dim N=d and the leaves of the foliation are of dimension pp. We set k:=d−pk:=d-p. We will take NN compact to avoid having to employ differential forms with compact support. We assume that NN is orientable and an orientation has been chosen. For clarity, let us employ adapted coordinates (xa,yα,d​xb)(x^{a},y^{\alpha},\textnormal{d}x^{b}) on Π​A⊂Π​𝖳​N\Pi A\subset\Pi{{T}}N. We select a classical Ruelle–Sullivan current, i.e., we define (locally)

(3.16) τ⁡(α):=∫Ndp​x​dk​y​μ​(y)​αp​(x,y).\tau(\alpha):=\int_{N}\textnormal{d}^{p}x\,\textnormal{d}^{k}y~\mu(y)\,\alpha_{p}(x,y)\,.

As we take NN to be compact, τ⁡(ℒXℱ​α)=0\tau\big(\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X}\alpha\big)=0, where ℒXℱ:=[dℱ,iX]\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X}:=[\textnormal{d}_{\mathcal{F}},i_{X}], where X∈𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍ℱ​(N)X\in{Vect}_{\mathcal{F}}(N). Suppose that for any n≥1n\geq 1 we have a collection of vector fields tangent to the leaves 𝑿:={X1,X2,⋯,Xn}\bm{X}:=\{X_{1},X_{2},\cdots,X_{n}\} that pairwise commute, i.e. [Xi,Xj]=0[X_{i},X_{j}]=0. We then define

(3.17) ϕ𝑿n(α0,α1,⋯,αn):=∑σ∈Snsgn(σ)τ(α0⋆ℒXσ⁡(1)ℱα1⋆⋯⋆ℒXσ⁡(n)ℱαn).\phi^{n}_{\bm{X}}(\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{n}):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\,\tau\big(\alpha_{0}\star\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X_{\sigma(1)}}\alpha_{1}\star\cdots\star\mathcal{L}^{\mathcal{F}}_{X_{\sigma(n)}}\alpha_{n}\big)\,.

Note that the Lie derivatives (as vector fields on Π​A\Pi A) are (shifted) even. We observe that the above is an application of Connes’ construction of a cyclic nn-cocycle from an invariant trace and commuting derivations (see [10]). Thus, ϕ𝑿n\phi^{n}_{\bm{X}} defines a derived cyclic nn-cocycle.

We remark that Connes applied cyclic cohomology to the noncommutative convolution algebra constructed from the holonomy groupoid of a foliation (see [11]). The derived cyclic cohomology is quite different and built from functionals of leaf-wise pseudo-differential forms.

Example 3.13.

Let NN be a compact manifold with a free and proper action of the Lie group TpT^{p}. By the Quotient Manifold Theorem, the orbit space N/TpN/\penalty T^{p} is a smooth manifold and N→N/TpN\rightarrow N/\penalty T^{p} is a smooth submersion; we of course obtain a principal bundle. In particular, we have a regular foliation whose leaves are diffeomorphic to TpT^{p}. It is a standard result that the Reeb class of such foliations vanishes - the foliation can be equipped with an auxiliary invariant metric rendering the foliation a Riemannian foliation. The Lie algebra of TpT^{p} is 𝔱≅ℝp\mathfrak{t}\cong{\mathbb{R}}^{p}. By choosing an ordered basis compatible with the integral lattice {e1,⋯,ep}\{e_{1},\cdots,e_{p}\}, we construct a global frame of fundamental vector fields 𝑿:={X1,⋯,Xp}\bm{X}:=\{X_{1},\cdots,X_{p}\} on NN using the standard method. These vector fields are tangent to the foliation and all pairwise commute, i.e, 𝔱\mathfrak{t} is abelian. For 1≤n<p1\leq n<p, we define all the possible subsets 𝑿n,i⊂𝑿\bm{X}_{n,i}\subset\bm{X} consisting of nn elements. We then define ϕ𝑿n,in\phi^{n}_{\bm{X}_{n,i}} via (3.17). For n=pn=p, we define ϕ𝑿p\phi^{p}_{\bm{X}}. Any change of ordered basis for 𝔱\mathfrak{t} is implemented on the fundamental vector fields via g∈𝖦𝖫⁡(p,ℤ)g\in\mathsf{GL}(p,{\mathbb{Z}}). Note det(g)=±1\det(g)=\pm 1. Thus, under change of the ordered basis we have ϕ𝑿p=det(g)​ϕ𝑿′p=±ϕ𝑿p\phi^{p}_{\bm{X}}=\det(g)\,\phi^{p}_{\bm{X}^{\prime}}=\pm\phi^{p}_{\bm{X}}. Thus, the derived cyclic pp-cocycle is canonical up to an overall sign (the orientation of TpT^{p}). From a starting basis, we have chosen an orientation of TpT^{p}, and we may consider changes of bases that respect the orientation and so det(g)=+1\det(g)=+1. With this restriction, the derived cyclic pp-cocycle is canonical (up to the choice of classical current).

Example 3.13 generalises as follows. Suppose we have a free and proper action of a compact Lie group GG on a compact manifold NN. As standard, we have a principal GG-bundle. The modular class of the associated foliation Lie algebroid vanishes; one can equip the foliation with an auxiliary invariant metric which can be used to construct a transverse invariant volume form and, in turn, a classical Ruelle–Sullivan current. The Cartan subalgebra 𝔱⊂𝔤\mathfrak{t}\subset\mathfrak{g} (the largest abelian Lie algebra within 𝔤\mathfrak{g}) generates a set of rr pairwise commuting vector fields via a choice of basis. Here rr is the rank of GG. We can then build derived cyclic nn-cocycles up to degree n=rn=r. The n=rn=r derived cyclic cocycle is canonical up to a non-zero scalar multiple determined by the choice of ordered basis of the Cartan subalgebra, i.e., up to the determinant of the change of ordered basis, and a choice of the classical current.

3.7. Applications to Deformations: Infinitesimal Deformations of Q-manifolds

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold and let X∈𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(M)X\in{Vect}(M) be an odd (infinitesimal) symmetry, i.e., an odd vector field that satisfies ℒX​Q=ℒQ​X=0\mathcal{L}_{X}Q=\mathcal{L}_{Q}X=0. It is well known that the deformation problem for homological vector fields is controlled by the differential Lie algebra (𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(M),[−,−],ℒQ)({Vect}(M),[-,-],\mathcal{L}_{Q}). That is, we can infinitesimally deform QQ using an odd (infinitesimal) symmetry, i.e., using an odd vector field that is ℒQ\mathcal{L}_{Q}-closed. We will return to this shortly.

Suppose we select a (non-zero) τ∈H​Cλ0​(M,Q)\tau\in HC^{0}_{\lambda}(M,Q). From this specified pair, we construct a derived cyclic 11-cochain

(3.18) ϕ⁡(f0,f1):=τ⁡((−1)f~0​X​(f0​f1))∈Cλ1​(M,Q).\phi(f_{0},f_{1}):=\tau\big((-1)^{\widetilde{f}_{0}}\,X(f_{0}f_{1})\big)\in C^{1}_{\lambda}(M,Q)\,.

A quick calculation, which we omit, shows that ϕ⁡(f0,f1)=−(−1)f¯0​f¯1​ϕ​(f1,f0)\phi(f_{0},f_{1})=-(-1)^{\overline{f}_{0}\overline{f}_{1}}\,\phi(f_{1},f_{0}), and so ϕ\phi is indeed shifted cyclic.

From the definition of the Hochschild coboundry operator (3.1), we have

Then using [Q,X]=0[Q,X]=0 and Lemma 3.1, i.e., τ∘Q=0\tau\circ Q=0, we obtain

∎

Using an odd infinitesimal symmetry, we can infinitesimally deform QQ as

Theorem 3.3.

Let (M,Q)(M,Q) be a Q-manifold, X∈𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(M)X\in{Vect}(M) be an odd infinitesimal symmetry, and τ\tau be a derived cyclic 00-cocycle. Then an infinitesimally deformed derived cyclic 00-cocycle τ(t)=τ+t​σ\tau_{(t)}=\tau+t\,\sigma exists if and only if the derived cyclic class [ϕ][\phi] is zero.

Proof.

Conversely, if ϕ=−b​σ\phi=-b\sigma for some σ∈Cλ0​(M,Q)\sigma\in C^{0}_{\lambda}(M,Q), i.e, [ϕ][\phi] is zero, then we may define τ(t)=τ+t​σ\tau_{(t)}=\tau+t\,\sigma such that b(t)​τ(t)=0b_{(t)}\tau_{(t)}=0. ∎

Definition 3.3.

The derived cyclic class [ϕ]∈H​Cλ1​(M,Q)[\phi]\in HC^{1}_{\lambda}(M,Q) defined by the derived cyclic 11-cocycle ϕ\phi (see (3.18)) is referred to as the deformation class of τ\tau along XX.

4. Concluding Remarks

We examined the notion of a derived product in the setting of Q-manifolds. As this multiplication is Grassmann odd, we require a shift in the grading to obtain what we referred to as a derived associative algebra. This derived product is inherently noncommutative. Alongside other results and constructions, we applied cyclic cohomology to the derived associative algebra. Note that this cohomology theory is distinct from the standard cohomology of a Q-manifold.

In standard cyclic cohomology applied to a noncommutative algebra, cyclic nn-cocycles are analogues of nn-dimensional de Rham currents, i.e., linear functionals on differential forms. Derived cyclic 00-cocycles are understood as BRST-invariant (shifted) traces. Derived higher cyclic nn-cocycles are interpreted as BRST-invariant currents, i,e., multi-linear functionals on functions that vanish on BRST-exact functions. It was shown that the infinitesimal deformation problem for derived cyclic 00-cocycles is controlled by the derived cyclic cohomology. A little more carefully, classes in H​Cλ1​(M,Q)HC^{1}_{\lambda}(M,Q) classify the obstruction to finding infinitesimally deformed cyclic 00-cocycles.

Future Directions:

  1. i)

    Explicit examples of derived cyclic nn-cocycles (n≥1n\geq 1) and derived cyclic cohomology groups require construction/calculation. Including (multi-)weights, for example ghost and antifield number, etc., may simplify the situation and give clearer links with physics and gauge mechanics. Moreover, the application of derived cyclic cohomology in the theory of (regular) foliations awaits proper exploration. However, as the derived associative algebra is non-unital, we realise that the standard methods/tools of calculating Connes’ cyclic cohomology cannot be directly applied (once the grading and shifted cyclic properties are taken into account). For example, the typical methods of Connes’ SBI sequence, mixed complexes using Connes’ periodicity operator, Morita theory, and application of the Künneth theorems, require the algebras to be unital. Thus, we either have to work with less standard frameworks that can cope with non-unital algebras, or adjoin a unit element (see Subsection 2.6). It must still be stressed that (standard) Hochschild cohomology and cyclic cohomology for noncommutative algebras are, in general, very difficult to calculate. In particular, it is common to have infinite-dimensional cochain complexes that grow exponentially in size, which make direct computations largely intractable.

  2. ii)

    We cannot directly use Künneth-type decompositions to simplify the calculation of the derived cyclic cohomology of a Q-manifold; for the case of cyclic cohomology of superalgebras see Kassel [19]. For one, the standard decompositions require the algebras to be unital, though this can be circumvented by the unitalisation as stated above. However, there is a more fundamental reason. Let us set A=(C∞(M1),⋆1)A=\big(C^{\infty}(M_{1}),\star_{1}\big) and B=(C∞(M2),⋆2)B=\big(C^{\infty}(M_{2}),\star_{2}\big) simply considered associative algebras. Then in the standard Künneth-type formula we encounter A⊗BA\otimes B (we ignore completions of the tensor product for this discussion), where the algebra is defined component-wise as

    (a1⊗b1)⋆(a2⊗b2)=±(a1⋆1a2)⊗(b1⋆2b2).(a_{1}\otimes b_{1})\star(a_{2}\otimes b_{2})=\pm(a_{1}\star_{1}a_{2})\otimes(b_{1}\star_{2}b_{2})\,.

    The issue is that this component-wise multiplication is structurally distinct from the derived product on C∞​(M1×M2)C^{\infty}(M_{1}\times M_{2}) generated by Q=Q1+Q2Q=Q_{1}+Q_{2}. In particular,

    (f1⊗f2)⋆(g1⊗g2)=(f1⋆1g1)⊗(f2​g2)±(f1​g1)⊗(f2⋆2g2),(f_{1}\otimes f_{2})\star(g_{1}\otimes g_{2})=(f_{1}\star_{1}g_{1})\otimes(f_{2}g_{2})\pm(f_{1}g_{1})\otimes(f_{2}\star_{2}g_{2})\,,

    as QQ acts as a derivation over the tensor product. This implies that “off-the-shelf” decompositions of the cohomology cannot be directly applied to derived cyclic cohomology. Thus, developing a modified Künneth-type isomorphism for derived cyclic cohomology is highly desirable to aid computations, assuming such an isomorphism exists. Developing the formalism in the context of differential graded algebras would allow the subtle issues with functional analysis to be avoided.

  3. iii)

    Formally, the notions and constructions of this work generalise to infinite-dimensional Q-manifolds such as the Fréchet or convenient supermanifolds of fields and antifields encountered in the BV–BRST framework. A rigorous treatment of the derived cyclic cohomology will require a restriction to local functionals to be applied to field theory. Developing ‘local derived cyclic cohomology’ may yield new algebraic invariants for classical gauge field theories and their space of observables.

In conclusion, derived cyclic cohomology of Q-manifolds ties to central ideas in differential geometry and mathematical physics. Given how prevalent Q-manifolds are, it is expected that further applications than those started here will be uncovered.
